0.title: Ezra: The God Who Rebuilds
0.overview:
The book of Ezra opens in the middle of a sentence. In most Hebrew Bibles Chronicles stands last, and its final words are a Persian king's decree breaking off at Let him go up. Ezra repeats the decree and finishes it: go up to Jerusalem, and rebuild the house of the LORD. The exile was a sentence God had not yet completed.

Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in the Hebrew canon, telling the story of the people who came home. Ezra is two stories a lifetime apart. Chapters 1-6 are the first return under Cyrus in 538 BC, led by Zerubbabel, the heir of David, and Jeshua the high priest: the altar rebuilt, the foundation laid to weeping and shouting, years of opposition, the preaching of Haggai and Zechariah, and the second temple dedicated in 516 or 515. Then Now after this (7:1) crosses fifty-eight years, the years of Esther, to 458 BC, when Ezra the scribe walks from Babylon with the law of God in his hand.

When did Ezra come? The traditional date is 458 BC, the seventh year of Artaxerxes I (7:7), thirteen years before Nehemiah (Neh 2:1). Some scholars argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, putting Ezra in 398 BC, after Nehemiah. But Ezra and Nehemiah appear together at the reading of the law (Neh 8:9), which fits the traditional order best, though the question is still debated.

Two things are invisible in an English Bible. Chapters 4-6 are not in strict date order: 4:6-23 gathers opposition from later reigns to show a pattern rather than an incident. And 4:8-6:18 and 7:12-26 are in Aramaic, the language of the Persian letters quoted.

The book is built on a few repeated words. God stirred the spirit of Cyrus and of the families who went home (1:1, 5). The hand of the LORD was on Ezra six times in chapters 7 and 8, each time explaining something that should not have happened. And Ezra set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel (7:10).

It ends on its hardest chapter. The returned community had married into households that served other gods (the issue was worship, not race; Ruth the Moabite is David's great-grandmother), and chapter 10 records the painful covenant to put those marriages away. A Christian reader must read it with the apostle's answer beside it: a believer married to an unbeliever should not divorce (1 Cor 7:12-14).

Through it all runs the God who rebuilds: he keeps the families' names, turns emperors' hearts, and brings his people back to the place where sin is dealt with. The house they built was smaller than Solomon's, but it was the one the Son of God walked into. And Zerubbabel stands in both genealogies of Jesus (Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27): David's line came home still waiting for its King.

1.title: The Stirred Heart: Cyrus, the Decree, and the Upward Call
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing:<sup>2</sup>"Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah.<sup>3</sup>Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel— he is the God who is in Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>And let each survivor, in whatever place he sojourns, be assisted by the men of his place with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts, besides freewill offerings for the house of God that is in Jerusalem."<sup>5</sup>Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem.<sup>6</sup>And all who were about them aided them with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered.<sup>7</sup>Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods.<sup>8</sup>Cyrus king of Persia brought these out in the charge of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah.<sup>9</sup>And this was the number of them: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers,<sup>10</sup>30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels;<sup>11</sup>all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up, when the exiles were brought up from Babylonia to Jerusalem.
1.overview: Ezra opens by finishing the sentence 2 Chronicles broke off. To fulfil Jeremiah's word the LORD stirs Cyrus, who proclaims that whoever belongs to the God of heaven may go up and rebuild his house, and those who stay must help (vv. 1-4). The same verb again: everyone whose spirit God had stirred rises to go, loaded with their neighbours' gifts as Israel was leaving Egypt (vv. 5-6). The temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar took are counted out to Sheshbazzar and carried home (vv. 7-11).
1.theology:
The chapter is built on one verb used twice. The LORD stirred up Cyrus (v. 1), and God stirred the families who went (v. 5). Providence opened the road; grace got particular people onto it. Neither the emperor's decree nor the exiles' decision is the first cause of the return. God is. Isaiah even calls Cyrus the LORD's anointed (Isa 45:1), a pagan king used for one task: he opened a road home from Babylon. The Anointed One, the Christ, opens the way home from a deeper exile, sin and death, and brings his people not to a ruined city but to God (1 Pet 3:18).

The return is written as a second exodus: a people leaving a foreign land with their neighbours' silver and gold (Exod 12:35-36), carrying the holy things, going up to the place of God's presence. And the vessels that had served as a pagan king's trophies are counted back to the last bowl — nothing given to God is finally lost to Babylon.
1.examples:
The last four words of 2 Chronicles are the middle of Ezra's third verse; the new book finishes the old book's sentence.

Cyrus's own clay cylinder credits Marduk. Scripture does not argue with it — it simply says who was moving him.

An emperor's permission opened the road, and it still took God stirring each family before anyone sold a house and started walking.

Those who stayed in Babylon were not condemned; they loaded the carts of the ones who went.

The cups Belshazzar drank from on the night Babylon fell were counted out by a Persian treasurer and carried back to Jerusalem.

The six items on the list add up to 2,499, and the total given is 5,400. Somebody counted, and the text keeps both figures.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The LORD Stirred Up the Spirit of Cyrus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Cyrus's first year, to fulfil Jeremiah's word, the LORD stirs the emperor, who proclaims that the God of heaven has charged him to build a house at Jerusalem (vv. 1-2); any of God's people may go up and rebuild it (v. 3), and those who stay are to help them (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The first three verses of Ezra are the last two verses of 2 Chronicles, almost word for word — and Chronicles breaks off at Let him go up. Ezra picks up the same sentence and finishes it: go up to Jerusalem, and rebuild the house.
verseByVerse.examples: Isaiah had named this king before he was born: who says of Cyrus, He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose (Isa 44:28). And Jeremiah had put a number on the exile — seventy years (Jer 25:11; 29:10). Verse 1 names Jeremiah's word, and Isaiah's came due in the same decree, in the mouth of a Persian who, as far as we know, had never read either. Because Isaiah names Cyrus so exactly, many modern scholars date Isaiah 40-55 to the exile; this commentary follows the traditional view, since the New Testament quotes those chapters as Isaiah's (John 12:38-41) and their argument is that God declares the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10).

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, so that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom and also put it in writing: "Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he has charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Whoever is among you of all his people, may his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and rebuild the house of the LORD, the God of Israel— he is the God who is in Jerusalem. And let each survivor, in whatever place he sojourns, be assisted by the men of his place with silver and gold, with goods and with beasts, besides freewill offerings for the house of God that is in Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reader coming straight from 2 Chronicles has read this before. Chronicles stops in the middle of Cyrus's proclamation, on Let him go up, and where Chronicles stands last those are the final words of the Old Testament.

Ezra finishes it: and rebuild the house of the LORD. The seam between the two books runs through a single royal decree, and the join is meant to be seen.

And verse 1 first tells us why it happened. Not because Persia had a policy of resettling conquered peoples, though it did, nor because Cyrus was generous, but that the word of the LORD by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled. Jeremiah had said seventy years while Jerusalem still stood and nobody believed him.

Cyrus himself left a clay cylinder, which still exists, crediting his conquest of Babylon to the god Marduk. The Bible does not argue with his inscription. It simply tells us who was actually moving him: the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus. A man can be the instrument of a God he has never met, and his own account of his motives is not the last word.

The decree has two halves: whoever wants to go, let him go, and whoever stays, let him help. Survivors is the word for the exiles now, the ones who came through, and the emperor has written the return and its funding into the same order.

Were Jeremiah’s seventy years fulfilled? Counted from the first deportation in about 605 BC to the return in about 538 BC, they come to some sixty-seven years, a round seventy that covers Babylon’s dominion, as Jeremiah said (Jer 29:10). Scripture also counts them another way, from the burning of the temple in 587 or 586 to its rebuilding in about 516 (Zech 1:12). Either way, the number God named was kept.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon in 539 BC and let exiled peoples go home. Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in the Hebrew Bible, covering about a century of return and rebuilding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Everyone Whose Spirit God Had Stirred
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those whom God had stirred rise to go up, and their neighbours load them with gifts (vv. 5-6). Cyrus brings out the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken, and his treasurer counts them out to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah, who carries them home (vv. 7-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The same verb runs through verses 1 and 5. God stirred the spirit of the most powerful man on earth, and God stirred the spirits of ordinary families in Babylon. The emperor's stirring produced a permission; theirs produced a journey. A decree can open a road, and only God can make anybody want to walk down it.
verseByVerse.examples: Add up verses 9 and 10 and they come to 2,499 vessels; verse 11 says the whole came to 5,400. The list probably names the principal pieces and the total counts everything, and the text does not explain the difference.

verseByVerse.quote: Then rose up the heads of the fathers' houses of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests and the Levites, everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem. And all who were about them aided them with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, with beasts, and with costly wares, besides all that was freely offered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone whose spirit God had stirred. It is the verb of verse 1 again, and the repetition is the whole theology of the chapter.

God stirred the spirit of an emperor, and the emperor produced a permission. But a permission moves nobody. Families who had been born in Babylon, who had houses there and vineyards and trades and grandparents buried there, had to decide to sell up and walk nine hundred miles to a city most of them had never seen, which was a ruin. What got them onto the road was the same hand that got Cyrus to pick up his pen.

That is the pattern of every return to God, then and since. Doors are opened by providence in the wide world — a decree, a circumstance, a chance. But nobody goes through a door because it is open. They go because something has been stirred in them, and the Bible never lets us take the credit for that part.

Not everyone went, and the text does not condemn those who stayed. Jeremiah himself had told the exiles to build houses and seek the welfare of the city (Jer 29:5-7). What it records is what the stayers did for the goers: they gave silver, gold, goods and beasts, besides freewill offerings.

Some are stirred to go, and some are stirred to load the cart. And Israel left Egypt carrying its neighbours' valuables too (Exod 12:35-36): a second exodus has begun, and it starts the way the first one did.

verseByVerse.quote: Cyrus the king also brought out the vessels of the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his gods. Cyrus king of Persia brought these out in the charge of Mithredath the treasurer, who counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah. And this was the number of them: 30 basins of gold, 1,000 basins of silver, 29 censers, 30 bowls of gold, 410 bowls of silver, and 1,000 other vessels; all the vessels of gold and of silver were 5,400. All these did Sheshbazzar bring up, when the exiles were brought up from Babylonia to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who has just finished 2 Chronicles watched the vessels go, in three loads (2 Chr 36:7, 10, 18). Nebuchadnezzar set them in his own temple as trophies, and on the last night of Babylon Belshazzar drank wine from them and praised gods of gold and silver while a hand wrote on the wall (Dan 5:2-5).

Now they come out counted: a named official on one side, a named recipient on the other, and a list between them. It is the same care with holy things that sent two men to empty Joash's chest together (2 Chr 24:11).

Do the sum on the inventory and it comes to 2,499, while verse 11 gives the whole as 5,400.

The text does not explain the gap, and it is more honest to say so than to pretend the figures agree. The likeliest reading is that the list names the principal pieces and the total counts everything that went back, including the smaller items nobody troubled to itemise. It is also true that numbers are the most fragile thing in any ancient manuscript; a single stroke changes a figure, and scribes copied these by hand for centuries. Nothing in the chapter turns on the discrepancy. What turns on the verse is that somebody counted.

Who was Sheshbazzar? He hands over the vessels here and then all but vanishes. Chapter 5 says he laid the foundations of the house (5:16); chapter 3 says Zerubbabel did (3:8-10). Some take them for one man with a Babylonian name and a Hebrew one; others for two leaders in succession. The text leaves it open, and so should we.

Every cup Belshazzar drank from was counted out, carried nine hundred miles, and delivered; nothing belonging to the house of God was written off as lost to Babylon. And that is how the Lord Jesus speaks of the people his Father has given him: this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day (John 6:39). He counts his people as the vessels were counted, and none is left behind in the house of another god.
verseByVerse.note: Sheshbazzar may be another name for Zerubbabel, or an earlier governor.
