2.overview: The roll of those who came home: eleven leaders headed by Zerubbabel and Jeshua, the lay families by clan and by town (vv. 1-35), then a host of priests against a handful of Levites, with singers, gatekeepers and temple servants (vv. 36-58). Some who could not prove their descent came anyway, and priests missing from the register were barred from the altar until God gave a word (vv. 59-63). The whole assembly is given as 42,360, and on arrival the families gave according to their ability to rebuild the house on its site (vv. 64-70).
2.theology:
The list is the answer to the exile's question. Babylon was meant to dissolve Israel into an empire, and generations later these families could still name their ancestors and their villages. God had not preserved an idea of Israel; he had preserved the sons of Parosh and the men of Anathoth.

Verses 59-63 hold law and mercy together. The unprovable are counted among the people; the unprovable priests are barred from the altar until God gives a word. The standard is not relaxed and nobody is thrown out, and the arrangement waits for a Priest whose office rests on an indestructible life (Heb 7:16).
2.examples:
Verse 2 names eleven leaders; Nehemiah's copy of the list has twelve.

The families added together come to 29,818; the stated total is 42,360, and the text keeps both figures.

A hundred and twenty-eight men of Anathoth came home to the town where Jeremiah had bought a field while Babylon was at the gates.

There were seventy-four Levites for 4,289 priests; the men with the hardest work mostly stayed behind.

A family called the sons of Sisera came home to serve at the altar.

A priest took the name of his famous father-in-law, and generations later his descendants could not find themselves in the register.

The first thing the families did on reaching the ruins was give money toward a building that was not there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–35 — The Men of the People of Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people who came up, each to his own town, under eleven leaders (vv. 1-2); the lay families counted by clan (vv. 3-20) and then by town (vv. 21-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The list is not an interruption of the story; it is the evidence the story needed. Babylon had been supposed to dissolve these families into an empire, and half a century and more later they could still tell you who their great-grandfather was and which village he farmed. God had not kept an idea of Israel through the exile. He had kept the sons of Parosh.
verseByVerse.examples: Anathoth is on the list — 128 men of it. That is Jeremiah's town, and while Babylon was besieging Jerusalem he bought a field there, paid in silver before witnesses, as God's pledge that fields would be bought and sold in this land again (Jer 32:15). Here are the buyers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these were the people of the province who came up out of the captivity of those exiles whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried captive to Babylonia. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each to his own town. Fifty to seventy years after the deportations, these families still knew which town was theirs. Most of the people walking back had never seen it; they were going home to a place they knew only as a name their grandparents used.

Modern readers skim a list like this, so it helps to know why the Bible keeps them. Every name was the answer to a question the exile had asked: whether Israel would survive as a people or melt into Babylon the way every other conquered nation had. This chapter is the answer, family by family.

Eleven leaders are named in verse 2, Zerubbabel and Jeshua at the head — the heir of David and the high priest, the two offices the community will be rebuilt around. Nehemiah's copy of the same list has twelve names (Neh 7:7), and twelve is probably the point: a returning Israel led by one man for each tribe. Somewhere in the copying of Ezra's list, one name has probably dropped out.

And the Nehemiah and Mordecai on the list are not the famous ones. The Mordecai of the book of Esther and the Nehemiah who rebuilt the walls were active decades later, in the 480s and the 440s BC. These are most likely other men who happened to share the name, and the text does not trouble to distinguish them because its first readers knew exactly who they were.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Parosh, 2,172. The sons of Shephatiah, 372. The sons of Arah, 775. The sons of Pahath-moab, namely the sons of Jeshua and Joab, 2,812. The sons of Elam, 1,254. The sons of Zattu, 945. The sons of Zaccai, 760. The sons of Bani, 642. The sons of Bebai, 623. The sons of Azgad, 1,222. The sons of Adonikam, 666. The sons of Bigvai, 2,056. The sons of Adin, 454. The sons of Ater, namely of Hezekiah, 98. The sons of Bezai, 323. The sons of Jorah, 112. The sons of Hashum, 223. The sons of Gibbar, 95.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eighteen family groups, 15,604 men, and the variation is the story. Some families came home two thousand strong, some with fewer than a hundred. Behind each figure is a set of decisions made in Babylon about who went and who stayed.

Somebody kept these records through generations in a foreign country, and that is itself a kind of faith: a family that goes on writing down its descent in exile expects to go home.

And God is interested in exactly this level of detail. He did not rescue the Jewish people in the abstract. He rescued the sons of Zattu, nine hundred and forty-five of them, and had it written down.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they may sometimes have been written with abbreviations or number signs; and the two lists may count slightly different things, such as those who registered and those who finally arrived. Neither touches what the passage teaches, and a copyist's slip in a figure does not unsettle the trustworthiness of what God has said; this commentary holds, with the historic confessions, that Scripture as first given is without error.

The list in Nehemiah 7 also differs in places; Nehemiah found and copied the old register (Neh 7:5), and some differences may come from updating it at a later date.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Bethlehem, 123. The men of Netophah, 56. The men of Anathoth, 128. The sons of Azmaveth, 42. The sons of Kiriath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743. The sons of Ramah and Geba, 621. The men of Michmas, 122. The men of Bethel and Ai, 223. The sons of Nebo, 52. The sons of Magbish, 156. The sons of the other Elam, 1,254. The sons of Harim, 320. The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 725. The sons of Jericho, 345. The sons of Senaah, 3,630.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the counting changes from the name of a family to the name of a town: fifteen entries, 8,540 men.

Bethlehem sends a hundred and twenty-three back to David's town, where Micah had said a ruler would come from (Mic 5:2). Five centuries later Herod's scribes read that verse to the wise men, and the ruler had been born there (Matt 2:5-6).

Anathoth is the one to stop at. It was Jeremiah's town (Jer 1:1), and during the last siege God told him to buy a field there, before witnesses, as a pledge: houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land (Jer 32:15). Here are a hundred and twenty-eight men of Anathoth walking home to farm it.

Bethel, where Jeroboam set up his calf, and Ai, where Israel lost its first battle because of one man's theft, are on the list too. Places with long and mixed histories, and the people coming home to them are not asked to account for any of it. And the largest group is the last: Senaah, 3,630, a town otherwise almost unknown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–63 — Priests, Levites, and Those Who Could Not Prove It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests (vv. 36-39), the few Levites, singers and gatekeepers (vv. 40-42), the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants (vv. 43-58); then those who could not prove their descent, and priests missing from the register who are barred until a priest with Urim and Thummim arises (vv. 59-63).
verseByVerse.theology: The priests who could not prove their descent were not expelled from the people. They were barred from the priesthood and told to wait for a word from God. Hebrews names the priest they were waiting for: one whose priesthood rests not on a register that can be lost but on an indestructible life (Heb 7:16).
verseByVerse.examples: Seventy-four Levites came home against 4,289 priests — about one to every fifty-eight. The men whose work was the heavy, unglamorous service of the house mostly stayed in Babylon, and when Ezra gathers his own caravan eighty years later he will look for Levites and find none (8:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua, 973. The sons of Immer, 1,052. The sons of Pashhur, 1,247. The sons of Harim, 1,017.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four priestly families, 4,289 men, roughly one in seven on the list. It was a return organised around a building that did not yet exist, and the families whose whole life was the altar came home in numbers.

The first is of the house of Jeshua, the high priest of verse 2. The line of Aaron has come through the exile unbroken, and its head stands beside the heir of David.

verseByVerse.quote: The Levites: the sons of Jeshua and Kadmiel, of the sons of Hodaviah, 74. The singers: the sons of Asaph, 128. The sons of the gatekeepers: the sons of Shallum, the sons of Ater, the sons of Talmon, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hatita, and the sons of Shobai, in all 139.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seventy-four Levites against 4,289 priests, when the whole temple system assumed the Levites would far outnumber them; they did the heavy work of the house, the carrying, cleaning, slaughtering and teaching.

The men whose service was hardest and least honoured mostly stayed in Babylon, and it is not hard to see why: a Levite had no land to go back to, only a job in a ruin. The shortage did not go away. When Ezra assembles his own caravan he finds none of the sons of Levi (8:15).

The singers are the sons of Asaph, the guild David set apart for the music of the house, still singing after two generations in a country where their harps hung on the willows.

verseByVerse.quote: The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, the sons of Hasupha, the sons of Tabbaoth, the sons of Keros, the sons of Siaha, the sons of Padon, the sons of Lebanah, the sons of Hagabah, the sons of Akkub, the sons of Hagab, the sons of Shamlai, the sons of Hanan, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Gahar, the sons of Reaiah, the sons of Rezin, the sons of Nekoda, the sons of Gazzam, the sons of Uzza, the sons of Paseah, the sons of Besai, the sons of Asnah, the sons of Meunim, the sons of Nephisim, the sons of Bakbuk, the sons of Hakupha, the sons of Harhur, the sons of Bazluth, the sons of Mehida, the sons of Harsha, the sons of Barkos, the sons of Sisera, the sons of Temah, the sons of Neziah, and the sons of Hatipha. The sons of Solomon's servants: the sons of Sotai, the sons of Hassophereth, the sons of Peruda, the sons of Jaalah, the sons of Darkon, the sons of Giddel, the sons of Shephatiah, the sons of Hattil, the sons of Pochereth-hazzebaim, and the sons of Ami. All the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants were 392.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the longest run of names in the chapter, and the most easily skipped: the temple servants, family after family, and the sons of Solomon's servants.

We know less about these people than about anyone else on the list. The temple servants are often connected with the Gibeonites, whom Joshua made cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD (Josh 9:27), and Solomon's servants with the non-Israelite peoples he conscripted as labour (2 Chr 8:7-9). If that is right, a good many of these families were not Israelite by descent at all. They had been attached to the house of God for centuries, and when the house was destroyed they went into exile with it, and now they are coming back to it.

One name in the middle of the list stops a reader: the sons of Sisera. It is the name of Jabin's general, the man Jael killed with a tent peg. Nothing in the text says this family descended from him. But a family carrying the name of Israel's old enemy is walking home from Babylon to serve at the altar of Israel's God, and the list gives them a line of their own.

All of them together come to 392 — a figure that includes families whose only claim on the house of God was that they had served in it. The book does not rank them below the priests. They are counted.

verseByVerse.quote: The following were those who came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, though they could not prove their fathers' houses or their descent, whether they belonged to Israel: the sons of Delaiah, the sons of Tobiah, and the sons of Nekoda, 652. Also, of the sons of the priests: the sons of Habaiah, the sons of Hakkoz, and the sons of Barzillai (who had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called by their name). These sought their registration among those enrolled in the genealogies, but they were not found there, and so they were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The governor told them that they were not to partake of the most holy food, until there should be a priest to consult Urim and Thummim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six hundred and fifty-two people who had lost their paperwork in the catastrophe and could not say for certain that they were Israelites came anyway. They are on the list. Nobody turned them back at the border.

One of the priestly families has a story. Barzillai the Gileadite fed David at Mahanaim when he fled from Absalom (2 Sam 19:31-39). Generations later a priest married into that famous family and took its name, and his descendants could no longer be found in the priestly register under their own.

Seeking their name and not finding it is one of the saddest sentences in the book.

Yet what was done was careful. They were not expelled from the people; they were barred from the priesthood and the most holy food and told to wait until there should be a priest to consult Urim and Thummim. Nobody in authority would decide by sentiment.

And for at least one family the waiting ended. Eighty years later the temple treasure was weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah (8:33), whose line Nehemiah gives as son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz (Neh 3:4). The sons of Hakkoz, unregistered in 538, were serving as priests by 458. The text never tells us how.

They were waiting, without knowing it, for a Priest of a different kind. Hebrews says Jesus came from Judah, a tribe Moses never connected with the priesthood, and is a priest not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16). The register that shut out the sons of Barzillai could not have admitted him either. His priesthood does not rest on a document that can be lost in a fire, and neither does the standing of anyone who comes to God through him.
verseByVerse.note: The Urim and Thummim, probably sacred lots kept in the high priest's breastpiece, were used to learn God’s will.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The total of the assembly, with servants, singers and animals (vv. 64-67); the families' freewill offerings for the house on its site, and everyone home to his own town (vv. 68-70).
verseByVerse.theology: They gave according to their ability: not a flat levy but proportion, the measure Paul uses of the Macedonians (2 Cor 8:3). And they gave not to buy their way back into God's favour but because he had already brought them home; the gift followed the rescue.
verseByVerse.examples: Add up the list and it comes to 29,818. Verse 64 says 42,360. The heading says it is counting the men of the people of Israel, so the likeliest reading is that the total takes in people the family lists never itemised. The text does not explain the gap, and it leaves both figures standing.

verseByVerse.quote: The whole assembly together was 42,360, besides their male and female servants, of whom there were 7,337, and they had 200 male and female singers. Their horses were 736, their mules were 245, their camels were 435, and their donkeys were 6,720.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole assembly together was 42,360.

Do the sum and it does not come out: every figure in the list adds up to 29,818, and the stated total is 12,542 higher. The heading counts the men of the people of Israel, so the likeliest reading is that the grand total takes in people the clan lists never itemised. Nehemiah's copy has the same total and different details. It is better to say so than to force the arithmetic.

And the animals are counted as carefully as the people, more than eight thousand beasts, most of them donkeys, which is what a column of families carrying everything they own over nine hundred miles actually looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the heads of families, when they came to the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, made freewill offerings for the house of God, to erect it on its site. According to their ability they gave to the treasury of the work 61,000 darics of gold, 5,000 minas of silver, and 100 priests' garments. Now the priests, the Levites, some of the people, the singers, the gatekeepers, and the temple servants lived in their towns, and all the rest of Israel in their towns.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of the LORD was a heap of burned stone. The first thing these families did on reaching it, before they had roofs over their own heads, was give money toward a building that was not there.

On its site: not a fresh start on cleaner ground, but the rock where Solomon's house had stood and David had bought a threshing floor. The return was not a new religion. It was the old one, rebuilt on its own foundations.

According to their ability, each in proportion to what he had, as Paul describes the Macedonian churches giving according to their means ... and beyond their means (2 Cor 8:3).

And the chapter ends quietly. Seventy verses of names, and the last one sends everybody home to start ploughing.

A roll of names like this one is the Old Testament's picture of something the Lord Jesus told his disciples to care about more than any success they could see. When they came back exhilarated from their first mission, he told them not to rejoice in what they had achieved, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Babylon could not blot out the sons of Parosh. Nothing can blot out a name he has written down.
verseByVerse.note: A daric was a gold coin of about 1/4 ounce and a mina about 1¼ pounds (ESV notes).

3.title: The Altar Before the Temple: Worship, Weeping, and the Shout of Joy
3.text: <sup>1</sup>When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God.<sup>3</sup>They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening.<sup>4</sup>And they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required,<sup>5</sup>and after that the regular burnt offerings, the offerings at the new moon and at all the appointed feasts of the LORD, and the offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD. But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid.<sup>7</sup>So they gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa, according to the grant that they had from Cyrus king of Persia.<sup>8</sup>Now in the second year after their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak made a beginning, together with the rest of their kinsmen, the priests and the Levites and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity. They appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to supervise the work of the house of the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And Jeshua with his sons and his brothers, and Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together supervised the workmen in the house of God, along with the sons of Henadad and the Levites, their sons and brothers.<sup>10</sup>And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their vestments came forward with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel.<sup>11</sup>And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel." And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.<sup>12</sup>But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house being laid, though many shouted aloud for joy,<sup>13</sup>so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.
3.overview: In the seventh month the returned families gather as one man, and the first thing they build is the altar, set in its place for fear was on them, with the daily offerings restored (vv. 1-3). They keep Booths as the law requires and restart the calendar of sacrifice, though the temple's foundation is not yet laid, and order cedar from Tyre as Solomon did (vv. 4-7). In the second year the foundation is laid, with trumpets and the old refrain of steadfast love (vv. 8-11). The old men who had seen Solomon's house weep, the young shout for joy, and the two sounds cannot be told apart (vv. 12-13).
3.theology:
The altar comes before the house. For twenty years the returned community worshipped at an altar standing among ruins, and the order is the gospel's: the place where sin is dealt with comes first, and the dwelling of God is built around it. And verse 3 makes fear the reason for worship, not the obstacle to it.

Verse 11 is the refrain sung when the cloud filled Solomon's house (2 Chr 5:13) and when the fire fell (7:3), now sung over bare foundation stones with neither. God's steadfast love was never true because the glory was visible.

Verses 12-13 hold grief and joy in one sound, and neither is rebuked. Haggai later granted the old men's grief in full (Hag 2:3) and answered it with a promise: the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former (Hag 2:9). The smaller house was the one the Son of God stood in.
3.examples:
The first thing the returnees built in Jerusalem was an altar in the open air on a hill of rubble.

They built it because they were afraid, and the text says so.

The Booths offering runs thirteen bulls, twelve, eleven — a countdown to seven — and the exiles kept it to the bull.

The cedar came from Lebanon by sea to Joppa, paid for in food, exactly as in Solomon's day.

Levites from twenty years old is David's rule, laid down in his last words (1 Chr 23:27).

Anyone old enough to remember the first temple standing was nearly sixty or older, and could see from the trench how much smaller the second would be.

The shouting and the weeping made one noise, and the noise brought the adversaries.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Set the Altar in Its Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the seventh month the people gather in Jerusalem as one man (v. 1). Jeshua the priest and Zerubbabel build the altar as it is written in the Law of Moses (v. 2), and they set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and the morning and evening offerings begin again (v. 3). They keep Booths with its offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required, then the regular offerings and the freewill gifts (vv. 4-5) — But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid (v. 6). They pay masons and carpenters, and send food, drink and oil to Tyre and Sidon for cedar floated to Joppa under Cyrus's grant (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The altar comes before the house. Before there are walls or a roof, the people restore the place where sin is dealt with. Access to God is not the reward for finishing the building; it is the first thing, and everything else is built around it. Yet the smoke had to rise every day, because no lamb could finish the work. Hebrews draws the contrast: every priest stands daily offering sacrifices that can never take away sins, but Christ offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins and sat down (Heb 10:11-12).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 gives fear as the reason for the altar, not an obstacle to it: they set it up for fear was on them. A frightened people did not wait until they felt safe to worship. They worshipped because they did not.

verseByVerse.quote: When the seventh month came, and the children of Israel were in the towns, the people gathered as one man to Jerusalem. Then arose Jeshua the son of Jozadak, with his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel with his kinsmen, and they built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings on it, as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God. They set the altar in its place, for fear was on them because of the peoples of the lands, and they offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, burnt offerings morning and evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh month is the holy month of Israel's year: trumpets, the Day of Atonement, Booths (Lev 23). The families of the last chapter have barely unpacked in their villages, and when the month comes round they walk back up to Jerusalem together.

What they build first tells you everything: not houses, not walls, not the temple, which will not stand for twenty years, but an altar on the ruins, in the open air. When the work is an altar the high priest's name comes first. And after half a century without one, nobody improvises: as it is written.

For fear was on them. The fear is not an obstacle they overcame; it is given as the reason. A few thousand families in a ruined city surrounded by peoples who did not want them there, and so they built the altar.

This is what faith does with fear. It does not wait to feel safe before it worships; it goes to the one place where the frightened are met by God. Whoever is afraid tonight has the same instruction, and a better altar: do not first fix the fear; go to the God who has already dealt with your sin.

And the offering goes up morning and evening, the daily sacrifice that stopped when Ahaz shut the doors (2 Chr 29:7) and again when the house burned. For the first time in two generations there is smoke over Jerusalem that is not the smoke of a burning city.
verseByVerse.note: The seventh month (September–October) held the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement and Booths. Jeshua the high priest is called Joshua in Haggai and Zechariah.

verseByVerse.quote: And they kept the Feast of Booths, as it is written, and offered the daily burnt offerings by number according to the rule, as each day required, and after that the regular burnt offerings, the offerings at the new moon and at all the appointed feasts of the LORD, and the offerings of everyone who made a freewill offering to the LORD. From the first day of the seventh month they began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD. But the foundation of the temple of the LORD was not yet laid. So they gave money to the masons and the carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and the Tyrians to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea, to Joppa, according to the grant that they had from Cyrus king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Booths was the feast when Israel lived for a week in shelters made of branches to remember the wilderness. For these people it hardly needed acting out; most of them were still living in something temporary.

By number according to the rule. The law for that feast is precise to the point of strangeness. On the first day, thirteen bulls. On the second, twelve. One fewer every day, down to seven on the seventh: seventy bulls across the week (Num 29:13-32). The offering is a countdown, and the returned exiles kept it bull by bull. People who have just come back from losing everything to their own unfaithfulness do not treat the details as optional.

Then the whole calendar restarted, and people gave freewill offerings beyond what it asked.

An altar standing by itself on a hill of rubble, smoke rising twice a day, and all around it the burned stones of the house. Worship had come back before the building did.

The cedar is Solomon's contract almost clause for clause: payment in food to Tyre, timber in rafts by sea to Joppa (2 Chr 2:10, 16). The second house is begun exactly the way the first one was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Sound Was Heard Far Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the second year the work begins under Levites from twenty years old (vv. 8-9). At the laying of the foundation priests and singers praise the LORD with the old refrain, and the people shout (vv. 10-11); the old men weep, others shout for joy, and the sound is heard far away (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The song in verse 11 is the one Israel sang when the cloud filled Solomon's house so that the priests could not stand to minister (2 Chr 5:13), and again when the fire came down (7:3). Here there is no cloud and no fire — only a row of foundation stones in a ruined city — and they sing exactly the same words. His steadfast love endures forever did not depend on the glory being visible.
verseByVerse.examples: Both sounds were right. The old men were not faithless for weeping; they knew what had been lost and could see from the size of the foundation how much smaller this house would be. The young were not shallow for shouting; they had been born in exile, and any foundation at all was a miracle. God's people have always lived with both sounds at once, and this is the verse that gives them permission.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the second year after their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak made a beginning, together with the rest of their kinsmen, the priests and the Levites and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity. They appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to supervise the work of the house of the LORD. And Jeshua with his sons and his brothers, and Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together supervised the workmen in the house of God, along with the sons of Henadad and the Levites, their sons and brothers. And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their vestments came forward with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the LORD, according to the directions of David king of Israel. And they sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD, "For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel." And all the people shouted with a great shout when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second month. Solomon, too, began to build in the second month (2 Chr 3:2). The writer keeps setting the new house down on the pattern of the old one.

The age of twenty is not an emergency concession. Moses set the Levites' service from twenty-five (Num 8:24), and David at the end of his life moved it to twenty: by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward (1 Chr 23:27). With seventy-four Levites in the whole caravan, they needed every one.

The sons of Asaph, the singers of 2:41, play the instruments their ancestors played, according to the directions of David.

A reader who has come through Chronicles knows that song. The Levites sang it when the ark came to Jerusalem. They sang it at the dedication of Solomon's house, and at the moment they sang it the house was filled with a cloud, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of God (2 Chr 5:13-14). The people sang it again on their faces when fire fell from heaven on the altar (7:3). Jehoshaphat's choir sang it marching out in front of his army (20:21).

Now it is sung over a row of foundation stones. There is no cloud. There is no fire. There is no ark, and there never will be again. And they sing exactly the same words, and add two of their own: toward Israel. His steadfast love endures forever, toward us — toward the people who were sent into exile for their sins and have just walked home.

That is what it means to believe the refrain. It was true in Babylon, where there was no altar at all, and on a building site, and on the worst morning of anyone's life. And the people's great shout is the phrase used of Jericho (Josh 6:5).

Haggai dates the laying of the foundation to 520 BC (Hag 2:18), but here it is the second year after the return, probably about 536. The likeliest answer is that the foundation was first laid then; when the work resumed in 520 after sixteen years of neglect, the foundation was laid again, or completed.

verseByVerse.quote: But many of the priests and Levites and heads of fathers' houses, old men who had seen the first house, wept with a loud voice when they saw the foundation of this house being laid, though many shouted aloud for joy, so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the joyful shout from the sound of the people's weeping, for the people shouted with a great shout, and the sound was heard far away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Old men who had seen the first house. Do the arithmetic: Solomon's temple was burned in 587 or 586, and this foundation is laid about fifty years later. Anyone who could remember that building standing was now nearing sixty at least, and had seen it as a boy. They had walked in its courts holding a father's hand. They remembered the size of it, the gold, the bronze pillars, the crowds at the feasts.

And they could see from the foundation lines how big this one would be. Not vague nostalgia but a measurement: the trench was marked out in front of them, and it was smaller.

The prophet Haggai spoke to exactly these men sixteen years later, and he did not pretend. Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes? (Hag 2:3). He granted every word of their grief.

And the young men shouted. Born in Babylon, they had no gold on the walls to measure against, only the promise that God would bring his people back, and here was a foundation to prove it. They were right too.

Anyone a little way off heard one noise, and could not have told whether Jerusalem was celebrating or grieving. It was doing both, at full volume.

It is as honest a picture of the church as the Old Testament gives: people who remember better days and grieve the gap, and people who see only the grace of what God is doing now. A church that only shouts has forgotten what was lost; a church that only weeps has forgotten who laid the foundation. The book does not ask either group to be quiet.

And the sound carried: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard (4:1). Joy in God's work is audible a long way off, and not everyone who hears it is glad.

The old men wept because this house would be smaller than Solomon's, and Haggai answered them with a promise they could not have understood: The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former (Hag 2:9). It was. Solomon's temple had the gold and the cloud; it never had the Son of God in it. This one did. Into this house, rebuilt and enlarged but still the second house, a baby was carried to be presented, and a twelve-year-old sat among the teachers asking questions, and a grown man drove out the money-changers and said it was his Father's house. The old men mourned a building that was smaller. They had just laid the foundation of the only temple the Lord of the temple ever walked into.

4.title: The Long Delay: Opposition, Discouragement, and Silence
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel,<sup>2</sup>they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here."<sup>3</sup>But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us."<sup>4</sup>Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build<sup>5</sup>and bribed counselors against them to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.<sup>6</sup>And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.<sup>7</sup>In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic and translated.<sup>8</sup>Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows:<sup>9</sup>Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates, the judges, the governors, the officials, the Persians, the men of Erech, the Babylonians, the men of Susa, that is, the Elamites,<sup>10</sup>and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River.<sup>11</sup>(This is a copy of the letter that they sent.) "To Artaxerxes the king: Your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River, send greeting. And now<sup>12</sup>be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.<sup>13</sup>Now be it known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired.<sup>14</sup>Now because we eat the salt of the palace and it is not fitting for us to witness the king's dishonor, therefore we send and inform the king,<sup>15</sup>in order that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find in the book of the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, hurtful to kings and provinces, and that sedition was stirred up in it from of old. That was why this city was laid waste.<sup>16</sup>We make known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls finished, you will then have no possession in the province Beyond the River."<sup>17</sup>The king sent an answer: "To Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, greeting. And now<sup>18</sup>the letter that you sent to us has been plainly read before me.<sup>19</sup>And I made a decree, and search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it.<sup>20</sup>And mighty kings have been over Jerusalem, who ruled over the whole province Beyond the River, to whom tribute, custom, and toll were paid.<sup>21</sup>Therefore make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me.<sup>22</sup>And take care not to be slack in this matter. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the king?"<sup>23</sup>Then, when the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease.<sup>24</sup>Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
4.overview: When the adversaries hear the building, they offer to join it — we worship your God as you do — and are refused, because they are the resettled peoples of 2 Kings 17 who feared the LORD and served their own gods as well (vv. 1-3). So they weaken the builders' hands, frighten them and bribe officials against them for the rest of Cyrus's reign and into Darius's (vv. 4-5). Then the chapter leaps forward: an accusation under Xerxes (v. 6), and under Artaxerxes a letter — given in the Aramaic it was written in — warning that the Jews are rebuilding the rebellious city's walls and will stop paying tribute (vv. 7-16). The king searches, finds the charge true, and stops the work until a decree is made by me; the officials enforce it by force (vv. 17-23). Verse 24 returns to the temple: the work ceased until the second year of Darius.
4.theology:
The first opposition is an offer of help. The refusal in verse 3 is of a partnership with a mixed religion, not of people: 6:21 welcomes anyone who separates from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD. The test was never whether others used the name of God but whether they wanted God alone.

Verses 6-23 are arranged by theme, not date, so that ninety years of opposition can be seen whole. And the accusation that finally works is a true one: Jerusalem had rebelled. The accuser rarely needs to lie; he only reads the record aloud when God's people try to build. The answer is not denial but the verdict of Zechariah 3 and Romans 8 — the filthy garments removed, and it is God who justifies.
4.examples:
The narrator calls them adversaries before they say a single friendly word.

They admitted in their own offer that Assyria had brought them there.

Fear drove the returnees to the altar in chapter 3 and off the building site in chapter 4.

From verse 8 the book is written in Aramaic, the language of the Persian letters it quotes, and stays in it until 6:18.

The accusers' letter was accurate about Jerusalem's past, and the king's archive confirmed it — and also confirmed that mighty kings once ruled the whole region from there.

The order that stopped the walls said until a decree is made by me, and the same king later sent Nehemiah to build them.

The foundation lay in the ground for sixteen years.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Let Us Build with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The adversaries offer to help build, claiming to worship the same God, and Zerubbabel refuses on the ground of Cyrus's commission (vv. 1-3). So they weaken and frighten the builders and bribe officials against them until Darius (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The offer sounded like worship, and the history behind it was the one told in 2 Kings: peoples resettled in Samaria by Assyria who feared the LORD but also served their own gods (2 Kgs 17:33). What was refused was a joint building with a mixed religion, not a person who wanted God — the Passover at 6:21 welcomes every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land.
verseByVerse.examples: The most dangerous opposition in this chapter is the first, and it arrives smiling. Nobody threatens anyone in verse 2. They offer to help, and they use the right words to do it. The threats come only after the help has been declined, which tells you what the help was for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel, they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of fathers' houses and said to them, "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to him ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria who brought us here." But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of fathers' houses in Israel said to them, "You have nothing to do with us in building a house to our God; but we alone will build to the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last chapter ended with a sound heard far away (3:13), and this is who heard it. The writer calls them adversaries before they open their mouths; nothing they are about to say will sound like it.

It is a generous-sounding offer, and it contains its own history. Who brought us here. These are the descendants of the peoples Assyria planted in Samaria after it emptied the northern kingdom, brought in from Babylon, Cuthah, Hamath and elsewhere (2 Kgs 17:24). Esarhaddon (about 681-669 BC) seems to have added settlers of his own a generation later, which is why they name him. And the book of Kings describes their religion in one sentence: they feared the LORD but also served their own gods (17:33), and their children and grandchildren did the same to this day (17:41).

So we worship your God as you do is half true, and the missing half is the whole point. They worshipped the LORD as one god among several, and building his house together would have meant building it as one shrine among several.

To a modern ear that sounds hard, and it needs to be read carefully, because the rest of the book tells us what it did not mean. It did not mean that nobody from outside could ever join them. Two chapters later the Passover is eaten by the returned exiles and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD (6:21). Anyone could come in who came to the LORD alone.

What was refused was a partnership with a religion that kept its other gods, and the ground given is the commission itself: as King Cyrus the king of Persia has commanded us. They had no authority to subcontract it.

Churches meet this offer still, and it still comes with the right vocabulary. Not every invitation to build together is an invitation to build the same thing. The test is not whether the other party uses the name of God, but whether they want God alone.

The quarrel these verses begin ran on for centuries, and the Lord Jesus walked into the middle of it. To a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well he said plainly that salvation is from the Jews, and then opened a door neither side expected: the hour was coming when true worshippers would worship the Father in spirit and truth (John 4:22-23). Christ gathers people from both sides into one worship of the one God, through himself.
verseByVerse.note: These adversaries were settlers brought in by Assyria — in part forerunners of the Samaritans.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build and bribed counselors against them to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Discouraged is literally that they weakened the hands of the people of Judah, the capacity to work. In the last chapter fear drove these people to the altar (3:3); now it drives them off the building site. The same emotion, with opposite results, depending on where it was carried.

Bribed counsellors, working the officials year after year: not a mob with torches but a funded, patient campaign of some sixteen years. It worked. The foundation laid with such noise sat in the ground, and nothing went up on it.

That is how most good work of God is stopped in practice. Not by a single catastrophe but by a steady pressure that makes it slightly harder every week, until the people who began it with shouting have quietly gone back to their own affairs. Haggai will arrive to tell them exactly that: they were living in panelled houses while the house of God lay in ruins (Hag 1:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–24 — Be It Known to the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under Ahasuerus an accusation is lodged (v. 6); under Artaxerxes a letter in Aramaic warns that the Jews are rebuilding a rebellious city that will stop paying tribute (vv. 7-16). The king searches the records, finds the charge true, and stops the work until he decrees otherwise, and it is stopped by force (vv. 17-23). Verse 24 returns to the temple, halted until Darius's second year.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 6-23 leap forward in time. Ahasuerus is Xerxes, who reigned a generation after the temple was finished, and Artaxerxes after him; their letters concern the city wall, not the house of God. Verse 24 then steps back to the temple in Darius's day. The writer has gathered ninety years of opposition into one chapter so the reader sees the pattern whole: whenever God's people build, someone writes to the king. For orientation, the Persian kings behind these chapters, with approximate dates, are Cyrus (took Babylon in 539, died 530), Cambyses (530-522, not named in Ezra), Darius I (522-486), Xerxes, the Ahasuerus of Esther (486-465), and his son Artaxerxes I (465-424).
verseByVerse.examples: The worst thing about the letter is that its history was accurate. Jerusalem had rebelled; its last king broke an oath sworn by God to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chr 36:13). The accusers did not need to lie. They took Judah's real past and used it to forbid Judah's future, and the king's own research confirmed every word.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. In the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam and Mithredath and Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic and translated. Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows: Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their associates, the judges, the governors, the officials, the Persians, the men of Erech, the Babylonians, the men of Susa, that is, the Elamites, and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River. (This is a copy of the letter that they sent.) "To Artaxerxes the king: Your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River, send greeting. And now be it known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations. Now be it known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and the walls finished, they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired. Now because we eat the salt of the palace and it is not fitting for us to witness the king's dishonor, therefore we send and inform the king, in order that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. You will find in the book of the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, hurtful to kings and provinces, and that sedition was stirred up in it from of old. That was why this city was laid waste. We make known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls finished, you will then have no possession in the province Beyond the River."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chapter jumps forward in time, and a careful reader must notice or the rest will not make sense.

And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. Ahasuerus is Xerxes, the king of the book of Esther, who came to the throne about thirty years after the temple was finished. Then verse 7: In the days of Artaxerxes — his son, later still. And what the Artaxerxes letter complains about is not the temple but the city: they are finishing the walls and repairing the foundations.

The writer is not confused about the order of the Persian kings. He has gathered opposition from ninety years into one chapter to show the reader that it was not an incident but a pattern. Whenever the people of God began to build anything in Jerusalem — the temple under Darius, the walls under Artaxerxes — somebody wrote to the king. Verse 24 will step back to the temple and pick up the thread from verse 5.

From verse 8 onward the book itself is written in Aramaic, the language of the Persian chancery, until 6:18. The letters are given in the language they were sent in.

The letter itself is a small masterpiece. It opens by listing everyone who signed it — officials, judges, Persians, men of Erech and Babylon and Susa, all the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported (probably Ashurbanipal of Assyria, about 668-627 BC) — so that the king sees a whole province of loyal subjects on one side and a few Jews on the other.

And it was true. Jerusalem had rebelled; its last king broke an oath sworn by God to Nebuchadnezzar (2 Chr 36:13), and the city was burned for it.

There is an accuser who works the same way. He rarely needs to lie about a believer's history. He only needs to read it out, accurately, at the moment the believer is trying to build something for God, and suggest that people with a record like that should not be allowed to start again.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 6–23 jump ahead to later opposition under Ahasuerus (Xerxes) and Artaxerxes before returning to the story. From 4:8 to 6:18 the book is written in Aramaic (ESV note), the language of Persian government.

verseByVerse.quote: The king sent an answer: "To Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, greeting. And now the letter that you sent to us has been plainly read before me. And I made a decree, and search has been made, and it has been found that this city from of old has risen against kings, and that rebellion and sedition have been made in it. And mighty kings have been over Jerusalem, who ruled over the whole province Beyond the River, to whom tribute, custom, and toll were paid. Therefore make a decree that these men be made to cease, and that this city be not rebuilt, until a decree is made by me. And take care not to be slack in this matter. Why should damage grow to the hurt of the king?" Then, when the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to the Jews at Jerusalem and by force and power made them cease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the middle of the royal reply is a sentence the accusers can hardly have wanted: mighty kings have been over Jerusalem. The Persian archives remember David and Solomon. The search meant to condemn Jerusalem turned up evidence of its glory as well.

Until a decree is made by me is a door the king left open without meaning to. Years later the same Artaxerxes will look at his cupbearer's sad face and give Nehemiah letters to rebuild these very walls (Neh 2:1-8).

In haste, and by force. That broken wall is probably the one Nehemiah heard about in Susa, which made him sit down and weep (Neh 1:3-4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem stopped, and it ceased until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With this verse the writer steps back to the story he left at verse 5. Nothing more was built on the house until Darius's second year, 520 BC, about sixteen years from the foundation.

Sixteen years. A child born the week the foundation was laid was a teenager before another stone went up. The altar still smoked morning and evening; the foundation lay in the ground with weeds growing in the trench. The people who had shouted over it got on with their farms.

This is one of the most honest verses in the Old Testament for anyone who has given years to a work of God that stalled. It records sixteen years of nothing, and does not hurry past them.

But it records them with an end date. The stoppage was real and not permanent, and the God who let it happen had already decided when it would end.

And the accusation of verse 15 was answered, in the end, not by proving it false but by God himself. The prophet Zechariah, who is about to appear in the next chapter, saw in a vision Jeshua the high priest — the same man who built the altar in chapter 3 — standing before the angel of the LORD in filthy clothes, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. The accusation was true; the clothes were filthy. And the LORD said, The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! ... Is not this a brand plucked from the fire? — and ordered the filthy garments taken off and clean ones put on (Zech 3:1-5).

That is still how the charge sheet is dealt with. Not by arguing that the record is exaggerated, but by the One who has taken the record away. Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died ... who indeed is interceding for us (Rom 8:33-34).
verseByVerse.note: Darius I reigned 522–486 BC; work resumed in his second year, 520 BC.

5.title: The Prophets Arise: Haggai, Zechariah, and the Resumption of Work
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them.<sup>2</sup>Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them.<sup>3</sup>At the same time Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and their associates came to them and spoke to them thus: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?"<sup>4</sup>They also asked them this: "What are the names of the men who are building this building?"<sup>5</sup>But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.<sup>6</sup>This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and his associates, the governors who were in the province Beyond the River, sent to Darius the king.<sup>7</sup>They sent him a report, in which was written as follows: "To Darius the king, all peace.<sup>8</sup>Be it known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands.<sup>9</sup>Then we asked those elders and spoke to them thus: 'Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?'<sup>10</sup>We also asked them their names, for your information, that we might write down the names of their leaders.<sup>11</sup>And this was their reply to us: 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished.<sup>12</sup>But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried away the people to Babylonia.<sup>13</sup>However, in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree that this house of God should be rebuilt.<sup>14</sup>And the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple that was in Jerusalem and brought into the temple of Babylon, these Cyrus the king took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor;<sup>15</sup>and he said to him, "Take these vessels, go and put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its site."<sup>16</sup>Then this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished.'<sup>17</sup>Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king for the rebuilding of this house of God in Jerusalem. And let the king send us his pleasure in this matter."
5.overview: After sixteen idle years, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah preach, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua rise up and start building, with the prophets beside them (vv. 1-2) — twenty-three days, by Haggai's dates, from his first sermon to the first stone (Hag 1:1, 15). At once the governor Tattenai comes asking who authorised it and who the builders are, but the eye of their God was on the elders, and the work goes on while the question goes to Darius (vv. 3-5). Tattenai's report is fair: a great house of huge stones, a work prospering in their hands (vv. 6-10). The elders' answer is honest to the point of confession — we are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and the first house fell because our fathers had angered the God of heaven — followed by Cyrus's decree, the returned vessels, and a request that the archives be searched (vv. 11-17).
5.theology:
The work of God restarts when the word of God is preached. Nothing in the political situation changed between chapter 4 and chapter 5; two prophets spoke, and Haggai describes the result with Ezra's own verb — the LORD stirred up the spirit of the leaders and all the remnant (Hag 1:14). The God who stirred an emperor by providence stirred his people by a sermon.

Verse 5 is watchfulness without guarantee: the builders did not know how Darius would answer, and they worked on under the eye of their God. And verse 12 shows the only safe way to hold a guilty past — confess it plainly. The accusers of chapter 4 had used Jerusalem's history as a weapon; here the builders name their fathers' sin themselves, and there is nothing left to use against them.

The two leaders the prophets stirred carried the two offices Israel's hope rested on, and the prophets lifted both beyond the men themselves. Haggai called Zerubbabel, the heir of David, God's signet ring (Hag 2:23), and Zerubbabel stands in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:12-13). Zechariah crowned Jeshua the priest as a sign of the man whose name is the Branch, who shall build the temple of the LORD and be a priest on his throne (Zech 6:11-13). The house they built was real stone. The King-Priest it pointed to builds a temple of his own body and of his people (John 2:19-21; Eph 2:21-22).
5.examples:
Haggai's first sermon was on the first of the month; the work restarted on the twenty-fourth.

His whole second oracle was one sentence: I am with you, declares the LORD.

The prophets did not preach and leave; they were on the building site, supporting the men they had rebuked.

The governor who came to investigate reported that the work was going on diligently and prospering.

The builders kept working for the weeks it took a letter to reach the king and come back.

Asked why their temple had been destroyed, they told a Persian official it was their own fathers' fault.

A trench full of weeds for sixteen years was described to the governor as the house being in building.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Eye of Their God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Haggai and Zechariah prophesy, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin to rebuild with the prophets supporting them (vv. 1-2). Tattenai asks who authorised the building and who the builders are, but God's eye is on the elders, and the work continues until Darius answers (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Sixteen years of nothing end in two verses, and what ends them is preaching. Haggai dated his first sermon to the first day of the sixth month (Hag 1:1), and on the twenty-fourth of the same month the people were back on the site — and Haggai uses the verb of Ezra's first chapter: the LORD stirred up the spirit of the governor, the high priest and all the remnant (Hag 1:14-15). The same God who stirred Cyrus stirred them again, and this time he did it through a sermon.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is the chapter's comfort. The inquiry was real and the builders had no idea how it would end, and they kept working while it was pending, because the eye of their God was on the elders. It is the watchfulness the seer Hanani described to Asa: the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chr 16:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied to the Jews who were in Judah and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel who was over them. Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, supporting them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sixteen years of silence end with two preachers. Nothing else had changed: the officials, the bribed counsellors and the weeds in the trench were all still there. What changed was that God spoke.

Haggai's sermons are not gentle. Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins? (Hag 1:4). The people said the time was not yet right (Hag 1:2); Haggai pointed out it had been right enough for their own carpentry, and told them to consider their ways.

Between that sermon and the work comes one of the shortest oracles in the prophets: I am with you, declares the LORD (Hag 1:13). The rebuke was followed by a promise, not a threat, and on the twenty-fourth day of the month the work began (Hag 1:15).

Haggai describes the moment with this book's own verb: the LORD stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel, of Joshua, and of all the remnant, and they came and worked on the house (Hag 1:14). The God who stirred Cyrus to write and the families to leave Babylon stirred them a third time.

And the preachers did not go home after preaching. The prophets of God were with them, supporting them, on the site, beside the men they had rebuked. Zechariah's word to Zerubbabel in those months names where the strength came from: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (Zech 4:6).

That is still how God restarts stalled work: by a word plainly spoken, and by his Spirit, who now lives in his people, giving them strength to obey it, with God beside them when they do.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and their associates came to them and spoke to them thus: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?" They also asked them this: "What are the names of the men who are building this building?" But the eye of their God was on the elders of the Jews, and they did not stop them until the report should reach Darius and then an answer be returned by letter concerning it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The timing is pointed. The builders had been at it for perhaps a few weeks when the regional governor arrived. After chapter 4 the reader braces for another round of accusation, and the question he asks sounds like it: Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure? And then, more ominously, What are the names of the men who are building this building? Writing down names is what officials do before arrests.

But it is a fair question. Tattenai governs a province for the Persian crown; a large building going up on the site of a city with a history of revolt is exactly the sort of thing he is paid to ask about. A Babylonian tablet from Darius's reign appears to name him with the same title. He is a real civil servant doing a real job.

The eye of their God. They did not know how the inquiry would come out. The last time letters went to a Persian king about Jerusalem, the work was stopped by force. And they kept building while the letter travelled, which was weeks each way at least, because the one watching them was not Tattenai.

The seer Hanani once told Asa that the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chr 16:9). Here that is, in the form of a provincial governor who decided, for reasons of his own, not to issue a stop order.

Anyone waiting on a decision they cannot control — a hearing, a result, a letter that could go either way — can take this verse personally. The outcome was not yet known. The eye was already on them. They went on working.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–17 — We Are the Servants of the God of Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tattenai's report describes the great house and the diligent work (vv. 6-10), and records the elders' answer: they serve the God of heaven, their fathers' sin brought the destruction, and Cyrus decreed the rebuilding and returned the vessels (vv. 11-16). Let the king search the archives (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Asked by a Persian official why their temple had been destroyed, the elders did not blame Babylon. They said their fathers had angered God, and God had handed them over. The accusers of chapter 4 had called Jerusalem a rebellious city; the builders went further than their accusers and named the real offence themselves. A people who can tell the truth about their own sin cannot be blackmailed with it.
verseByVerse.examples: Tattenai is not the villain the reader expects after chapter 4. He asks the right question, lets the work continue while he asks it, describes the building accurately and even admiringly, and asks the king to check the builders' claim rather than his own suspicions. An honest official is a gift of God, and the text takes the trouble to show us one.

verseByVerse.quote: This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the province Beyond the River and Shethar-bozenai and his associates, the governors who were in the province Beyond the River, sent to Darius the king. They sent him a report, in which was written as follows: "To Darius the king, all peace. Be it known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with huge stones, and timber is laid in the walls. This work goes on diligently and prospers in their hands. Then we asked those elders and spoke to them thus: 'Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this structure?' We also asked them their names, for your information, that we might write down the names of their leaders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The surprise in Tattenai's report is how fair it is.

The letter of chapter 4 called Jerusalem that rebellious and wicked city and went for the king's revenue. This one calls the building the house of the great God and reports that the work is prospering in their hands.

Even the names are taken for your information: a file, not a charge.

Not every questioner is an enemy. After a chapter of opposition a person can learn to hear every enquiry as an attack. Tattenai asked hard questions honestly and wrote down the answers straight, and God used his fairness as surely as the prophets' sermons.

verseByVerse.quote: And this was their reply to us: 'We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and finished. But because our fathers had angered the God of heaven, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house and carried away the people to Babylonia. However, in the first year of Cyrus king of Babylon, Cyrus the king made a decree that this house of God should be rebuilt. And the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple that was in Jerusalem and brought into the temple of Babylon, these Cyrus the king took out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered to one whose name was Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor; and he said to him, "Take these vessels, go and put them in the temple that is in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its site." Then this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the house of God that is in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been in building, and it is not yet finished.' Therefore, if it seems good to the king, let search be made in the royal archives there in Babylon, to see whether a decree was issued by Cyrus the king for the rebuilding of this house of God in Jerusalem. And let the king send us his pleasure in this matter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders' reply, as Tattenai records it, is a small sermon in its own right.

The first thing they say about themselves is servants: not subjects of Persia, but servants of the God who made heaven and earth, a large claim to make to a governor, and made before they mention anybody's decree.

Set that beside chapter 4. There the charge of rebellion worked because it was true. Here the builders go further than their accusers: not Babylon's doing, not bad luck, but our fathers angered God, and God handed them over.

That is the only safe way to hold a guilty past. A people who will tell the truth about their own sin, out loud, to a stranger, cannot be blackmailed with it. The accuser's leverage is always the thing we are hiding, and they had stopped hiding it.

Not yet finished is a kindly way of describing sixteen years of weeds. Haggai had put it differently (Hag 1:2). The elders did not lie, since the building had been begun and not abandoned in law, but they chose their words with care.

And they invite the check. In chapter 4 the archive was a weapon; here it is asked for by the people with nothing to hide.

They built on, not knowing what the search would find, with nothing to rest on but a decree they could not produce and a promise from Haggai that fitted into one line: I am with you, declares the LORD. It is the same promise the Lord Jesus gave to the church when he sent it out to build something far larger than a temple, with no decree it could show the world's governors except his word: And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20).

Verse 16 says Sheshbazzar laid the foundation, but chapter 3 names Zerubbabel. Sheshbazzar was the governor under whose authority it was laid (1:8), or the two names belong to one man.

6.title: The Temple Completed: Darius's Decree, Dedication, and Passover
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in Babylonia, in the house of the archives where the documents were stored.<sup>2</sup>And in Ecbatana, the citadel that is in the province of Media, a scroll was found on which this was written: "A record.<sup>3</sup>In the first year of Cyrus the king, Cyrus the king issued a decree: Concerning the house of God at Jerusalem, let the house be rebuilt, the place where sacrifices were offered, and let its foundations be retained. Its height shall be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits,<sup>4</sup>with three layers of great stones and one layer of timber. Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury.<sup>5</sup>And also let the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that is in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be restored and brought back to the temple that is in Jerusalem, each to its place. The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River.<sup>9</sup>And whatever is needed—bulls, rams, or sheep for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, or oil, as the priests at Jerusalem require—let that be given to them day by day without fail,<sup>10</sup>that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons.<sup>11</sup>Also I make a decree that if anyone alters this edict, a beam shall be pulled out of his house, and he shall be impaled on it, and his house shall be made a dunghill.<sup>12</sup>May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who shall put out a hand to alter this, or to destroy this house of God that is in Jerusalem. I Darius make a decree; let it be done with all diligence."<sup>13</sup>Then, according to the word sent by Darius the king, Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered.<sup>14</sup>And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia;<sup>15</sup>and this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.<sup>16</sup>And the people of Israel, the priests and the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles, celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy.<sup>17</sup>They offered at the dedication of this house of God 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs, and as a sin offering for all Israel 12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel.<sup>18</sup>And they set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their divisions, for the service of God at Jerusalem, as it is written in the Book of Moses.<sup>19</sup>On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles kept the Passover.<sup>20</sup>For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were clean. So they slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the returned exiles, for their fellow priests, and for themselves.<sup>21</sup>It was eaten by the people of Israel who had returned from exile, and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>22</sup>And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel.
6.overview: Darius has the archives searched, and Cyrus's memorandum turns up in Ecbatana: rebuild the house at royal expense and return the vessels (vv. 1-5). Darius tells Tattenai to keep away, pays the builders from the province's tribute, supplies the offerings so the priests will pray for the king, and seals the edict with a blessing in Deuteronomy's language (vv. 6-12).
