The house is finished through the prophesying of Haggai ... and Zechariah, some seventy years after the fire, and dedicated with a sin offering for all twelve tribes (vv. 13-18). The Passover follows on the right date, open to all who had left the uncleanness of the nations, for the LORD had made them joyful (vv. 19-22).
6.theology:
The chapter is a sequence of reversals, all of them God's. The archive the accusers invoked to prove Jerusalem guilty produces the decree that authorises it; the tribute they feared losing pays for the house; the empire that now rules the lands of the power that began the exile — the king of Assyria — funds the altar. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Prov 21:1).

And the writer credits the finished building not to Darius's money but to the prophesying of Haggai ... and Zechariah (v. 14). God's decree is named before the three kings'. The Passover that follows answers the refusal of chapter 4: the door was shut to a partnership with other gods and open to every person who left them to worship the LORD (v. 21).
6.examples:
They searched Babylon for the decree and found it three hundred miles away in a summer palace.

The tribute the accusers said Jerusalem would stop paying was spent on Jerusalem's temple.

A Persian emperor asked the Jews to pray for his life and his sons.

Solomon dedicated his house with 22,000 oxen; the returnees dedicated theirs with a hundred bulls, and made no apology.

A community from two tribes offered twelve goats, one for every tribe of Israel.

The Aramaic section of the book ends at the Passover, and the story goes back into Hebrew.

This time, every priest and Levite was clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cyrus's memorandum is found at Ecbatana: rebuild the house at royal cost and restore the vessels (vv. 1-5). Darius orders Tattenai to keep away, to pay the builders from the province's tribute and to supply the daily offerings, and he guards the edict with a penalty and a blessing (vv. 6-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 8 pays for the house out of the very revenue the accusers of chapter 4 warned the king he would lose (4:13).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 has a Persian emperor praying in the language of Deuteronomy: the God who has caused his name to dwell there is Moses' phrase for the place God would choose (Deut 12:11). Somebody in that chancery had heard it from the Jews, and the king signed it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in Babylonia, in the house of the archives where the documents were stored. And in Ecbatana, the citadel that is in the province of Media, a scroll was found on which this was written: "A record. In the first year of Cyrus the king, Cyrus the king issued a decree: Concerning the house of God at Jerusalem, let the house be rebuilt, the place where sacrifices were offered, and let its foundations be retained. Its height shall be sixty cubits and its breadth sixty cubits, with three layers of great stones and one layer of timber. Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury. And also let the gold and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that is in Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be restored and brought back to the temple that is in Jerusalem, each to its place. You shall put them in the house of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tattenai had asked the king to look in Babylon (5:17), and they looked in Babylon, and it was not there. It turned up three hundred miles away in Ecbatana, the old Median capital, where the Persian kings spent their summers. Someone had filed it there in Cyrus's first year and nobody had touched it since.

That is how providence often works: not by a voice from heaven but by a clerk who kept the archive properly, and a search that went on after the obvious place came up empty.

And what they found was not the proclamation of chapter 1 but the file copy: A record. The public announcement had spoken of the God of heaven and invited volunteers. The office memorandum adds what a treasury wants to know. Let the house be rebuilt, the place where sacrifices were offered, and let its foundations be retained. Dimensions, sixty cubits by sixty. Three layers of great stones and one layer of timber. And the line that mattered most in Darius's court: Let the cost be paid from the royal treasury.

Then the vessels again: be restored and brought back to the temple that is in Jerusalem, each to its place. Each to its place. Cyrus's clerks had not only counted them out; they had minuted that every basin was to go back where it came from.
verseByVerse.note: Ecbatana was a summer residence of the Persian kings. A copy of Cyrus’s decree was found there.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, Tattenai, governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates the governors who are in the province Beyond the River, keep away. Let the work on this house of God alone. Let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews rebuild this house of God on its site. Moreover, I make a decree regarding what you shall do for these elders of the Jews for the rebuilding of this house of God. The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River. And whatever is needed—bulls, rams, or sheep for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, or oil, as the priests at Jerusalem require—let that be given to them day by day without fail, that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. Also I make a decree that if anyone alters this edict, a beam shall be pulled out of his house, and he shall be impaled on it, and his house shall be made a dunghill. May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who shall put out a hand to alter this, or to destroy this house of God that is in Jerusalem. I Darius make a decree; let it be done with all diligence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Darius's reply to Tattenai goes far beyond what anyone had asked for.

Keep away. The governor who came to ask questions is told to stand back from the site. And then Darius adds his own decree on top of Cyrus's: The cost is to be paid to these men in full and without delay from the royal revenue, the tribute of the province from Beyond the River.

The tribute of the province. Turn back to the letter the accusers wrote in chapter 4: if this city is rebuilt ... they will not pay tribute, custom, or toll, and the royal revenue will be impaired (4:13). The revenue they were so anxious to protect is now paid out, by royal order, to build the very thing they were trying to stop.

And the reason: that they may offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. A Persian emperor wants the prayers of the Jews. It is exactly what Jeremiah told the first exiles to do in Babylon: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jer 29:7). Paul will tell the church the same about kings and all in authority (1 Tim 2:1-2). God's people have always been asked to pray for rulers who did not share their faith, and here a ruler asked for it himself.

The penalty clause is savage — anyone who alters the edict is to be impaled on a beam pulled from his own house — and it is Darius's, not God's. Persian kings did such things. The text records it without comment.

But the closing blessing is remarkable. May the God who has caused his name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who shall put out a hand to alter this. That is Deuteronomy's phrase — the place that the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there (Deut 12:11) — in the mouth of a Persian king. Somebody in the chancery had learned it from the Jews, and the emperor put his seal to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — The LORD Had Made Them Joyful
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tattenai obeys, and the elders build and prosper through the prophets, finishing the house in Darius's sixth year (vv. 13-15). It is dedicated with joy and a sin offering for the twelve tribes, and the priests are set in their divisions (vv. 16-18). The Passover is kept with every priest and Levite clean, shared with all who had separated themselves to the LORD, and the feast is kept with joy (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The house was burned in 586 and finished in 516 or 515 — some seventy years. Scripture itself counts the seventy more than one way: Jeremiah measured it as Babylon's dominion (Jer 25:11; 29:10), and Zechariah, preaching while this house was going up, spoke of God's anger on Jerusalem these seventy years (Zech 1:12). Either way, the God who named the number was still keeping it.
verseByVerse.examples: Twelve goats for twelve tribes, offered by a community drawn almost entirely from two of them: they made atonement for all Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Then, according to the word sent by Darius the king, Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered. And the elders of the Jews built and prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia; and this house was finished on the third day of the month of Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, according to the word sent by Darius the king, Tattenai ... did with all diligence what Darius the king had ordered. The fair official of chapter 5 does his duty promptly.

Through the prophesying. The writer has just printed two imperial decrees and a treasury order, and when he says what the building actually rose on, he names two preachers. The money came from Darius. The stones came from the quarries. The house was built through the word of God.

They finished their building by decree of the God of Israel and by decree of Cyrus and Darius and Artaxerxes king of Persia. God's decree is first, and the three kings follow it. Artaxerxes came to the throne some fifty years after this house was finished; his name is added because in the next chapter he will send gold and silver to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem (7:27). The writer lists every king who served the house, in whatever order they came.

The sixth year of Darius is 516 or 515 (the third of Adar probably fell in March 515), and Solomon's house was burned in 587 or 586: some seventy years from the fire to the finished house. Jeremiah spoke of seventy years of Babylon's rule (Jer 25:11; 29:10); Zechariah, preaching on this building site, asked how long God would be angry these seventy years (Zech 1:12). The number God had named came due in the time God had named.

From the first stone to the last, counting the sixteen idle years, it had taken about twenty-one. From Haggai's first sermon, four and a half.
verseByVerse.note: The temple was finished in 515 BC, about seventy years after its destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel, the priests and the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles, celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy. They offered at the dedication of this house of God 100 bulls, 200 rams, 400 lambs, and as a sin offering for all Israel 12 male goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel. And they set the priests in their divisions and the Levites in their divisions, for the service of God at Jerusalem, as it is written in the Book of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With joy. Some of the old men who wept over the foundation twenty-one years earlier were surely dead by now. Their grandchildren stood in the finished courts, and nobody is recorded as weeping.

A hundred bulls. At the dedication of Solomon's house, the king offered 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep (2 Chr 7:5). The returnees did not pretend to be Solomon. They offered what a small, poor community could offer, and the writer records it without apology.

But look at the twelve goats. The community that came home was drawn almost entirely from Judah and Benjamin, and it offered a sin offering for every tribe of Israel, one goat each. Hezekiah's great sin offering was seven goats (2 Chr 29:21). These people had every reason to think of themselves as the remnant of a remnant, and they would not let Israel shrink to their own size. They made atonement for the whole people, including the ten tribes scattered by Assyria two centuries earlier.

Then the priests and Levites are set in their divisions as it is written in the Book of Moses. And with that verse, the Aramaic section of the book ends. From 4:8 to 6:18 the story has been told in the language of the Persian letters. At verse 19 it returns to Hebrew — at the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourteenth day of the first month, the returned exiles kept the Passover. For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were clean. So they slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the returned exiles, for their fellow priests, and for themselves. It was eaten by the people of Israel who had returned from exile, and also by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD, the God of Israel. And they kept the Feast of Unleavened Bread seven days with joy, for the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria to them, so that he aided them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the right date. A reader who has just come through 2 Chronicles will remember that Hezekiah had to move his Passover to the second month, because the priests had not consecrated themselves in sufficient number (2 Chr 30:3), and that at the feast itself many were unclean and the Levites had to kill the lambs for them.

For the priests and the Levites had purified themselves together; all of them were clean. All of them. Not one priest unready, not one Levite short. The first Passover in the rebuilt house is the one where the clergy had dealt with themselves in good time.

Here is the verse that tells us how to read the refusal of chapter 4. The door was never shut to people. Anyone from the peoples of the land who turned from their gods to the LORD could sit down to this meal, exactly as the law had provided for the stranger at the first Passover in Egypt (Exod 12:48). What was refused in chapter 4 was a partnership with other gods. What is welcomed here is a person who has left them.

The LORD had made them joyful. Their joy is given, like everything else in this book: the spirits stirred in chapter 1, the sermons of chapter 5, the scroll in Ecbatana. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD; he turns it wherever he will (Prov 21:1), and he had turned it.

Darius is also called the king of Assyria. It is an old title for the power that ruled that empire's lands, and it names the kingdom whose armies began Israel's exile, carrying the northern tribes away two centuries before. The empire that started the scattering is now paying for the altar. The circle has closed.

The first half of Ezra ends with a lamb killed and eaten by a people who had come home, and with foreigners who had turned to God at the same table. It is the right place for it to end. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7), and the table he keeps is the same shape: exiles brought home, strangers who have left their gods, and a joy that nobody at it manufactured.

7.title: The Scribe-Priest Arrives: Ezra, the Law, and the Hand of God
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah,<sup>2</sup>son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub,<sup>3</sup>son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth,<sup>4</sup>son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki,<sup>5</sup>son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest—<sup>6</sup>this Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him.<sup>7</sup>And there went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants.<sup>8</sup>And Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king.<sup>9</sup>For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him.<sup>10</sup>For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.<sup>11</sup>This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, a man learned in matters of the commandments of the LORD and his statutes for Israel:<sup>12</sup>"Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace. And now<sup>13</sup>I make a decree that anyone of the people of Israel or their priests or Levites in my kingdom, who freely offers to go to Jerusalem, may go with you.<sup>14</sup>For you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to make inquiries about Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand,<sup>15</sup>and also to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem,<sup>16</sup>with all the silver and gold that you shall find in the whole province of Babylonia, and with the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly for the house of their God that is in Jerusalem.<sup>17</sup>With this money, then, you shall with all diligence buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings, and you shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God that is in Jerusalem.<sup>18</sup>Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God.<sup>19</sup>The vessels that have been given you for the service of the house of your God, you shall deliver before the God of Jerusalem.<sup>20</sup>And whatever else is required for the house of your God, which it falls to you to provide, you may provide it out of the king's treasury.<sup>21</sup>"And I, Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, requires of you, let it be done with all diligence,<sup>22</sup>up to 100 talents of silver, 100 cors of wheat, 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much.<sup>23</sup>Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full for the house of the God of heaven, lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons.<sup>24</sup>We also notify you that it shall not be lawful to impose tribute, custom, or toll on anyone of the priests, the Levites, the singers, the doorkeepers, the temple servants, or other servants of this house of God.<sup>25</sup>"And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges who may judge all the people in the province Beyond the River, all such as know the laws of your God. And those who do not know them, you shall teach.<sup>26</sup>Whoever will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be strictly executed on him, whether for death or for banishment or for confiscation of his goods or for imprisonment."<sup>27</sup>Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem,<sup>28</sup>and who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers. I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.
7.overview:
Fifty-eight years after the temple was finished, Ezra appears: a priest descended from Aaron through Zadok and Hilkiah, and a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses, to whom the king gives everything he asks, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him (vv. 1-7). The four-month journey goes under the good hand of God, for Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach it (vv. 8-10).

Artaxerxes' letter, given in Aramaic, commissions him to examine Judah by the law in his hand, funds the altar, exempts the temple staff from tax, and orders judges appointed and the ignorant taught (vv. 11-26). Then Ezra speaks in his own voice, blessing the LORD who put this into the king's heart (vv. 27-28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Hand of the LORD His God Was on Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra, a priest of Aaron's line and a skilled scribe, goes up from Babylon with a company of Israelites in Artaxerxes' seventh year, the king granting all he asks, for God's hand is on him (vv. 1-7). The journey takes four months, under God's good hand, because Ezra had set his heart on the law (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 explains verse 9 — it begins with for. The good hand of God was on Ezra, because Ezra had set his heart to study the law. And the order of the three verbs cannot be reversed: study first, then do, then teach. A man cannot teach honestly what he has not first obeyed, and he cannot obey what he has not first taken the trouble to know.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra's genealogy runs through Hilkiah, the high priest who found the lost Book of the Law in Josiah's temple (2 Chr 34:14; 1 Chr 6:13-14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now after this, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub, son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth, son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki, son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now after this. Three words, and fifty-eight years go by. Everything in the book of Esther happens in the gap between chapter 6 and chapter 7. The house has stood for two generations, and most of the people who dedicated it are dead.

The genealogy is not decoration. Ezra's line is traced back to Aaron the chief priest, through Phinehas and Zadok. It is selective, and son of means descendant: Seraiah, the first name, was the chief priest executed at Riblah in 586 (2 Kgs 25:18-21). His son Jehozadak went into exile (1 Chr 6:15), and his grandson was Jeshua, who built the altar in chapter 3.

And one name in the list should stop a reader who has just come through 2 Chronicles. Son of Hilkiah. First Chronicles puts Hilkiah two generations above Seraiah (1 Chr 6:13-14): he is the high priest of Josiah's reign — the man who, while the builders were carrying money out of a storeroom, found the Book of the Law of the LORD given through Moses (2 Chr 34:14).

The Bible had been lost in the house of God until Hilkiah found it. A century and a half later, the man who carries that same law back to Jerusalem and sets out to teach it to the whole nation is Hilkiah's descendant. Families carry more than blood. Somewhere in that line, through an exile and a burned temple, somebody kept telling the children about the book.
verseByVerse.note: Ezra came almost sixty years after the temple was finished, in 458 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: this Ezra went up from Babylonia. He was a scribe skilled in the Law of Moses that the LORD, the God of Israel, had given, and the king granted him all that he asked, for the hand of the LORD his God was on him. And there went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A scribe skilled. The psalmist has the picture: my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe (Ps 45:1). For Ezra the law of Moses was not a reference work but the language he thought in. His descent gave him his standing; his skill with the book gave him his usefulness.

The hand of the LORD appears six times in chapters 7 and 8 (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31), and every time it explains something that should not have happened. Why did the most powerful king on earth give a Jewish scribe everything he asked? Not because Ezra negotiated well.

And he did not go alone. There went up also to Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king, some of the people of Israel, and some of the priests and Levites, the singers and gatekeepers, and the temple servants. Every order of the temple community is represented again, as it was in chapter 2. A second return, smaller than the first, bringing the one thing the first had not brought with it in force: a teacher.

When did Ezra come? The traditional date is 458 BC, the seventh year of Artaxerxes I (7:7), thirteen years before Nehemiah (Neh 2:1). Some scholars argue that the king was Artaxerxes II, putting Ezra in 398 BC, after Nehemiah. But Ezra and Nehemiah appear together at the reading of the law (Neh 8:9) and at the dedication of the wall (Neh 12:26, 36), which fits the traditional order best. The strongest argument for the later date is a name: Ezra spends a night in the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib (10:6), and a high priest Johanan is known from papyri found at Elephantine in Egypt around 410 BC. But the name was common, and an earlier Jehohanan with a temple room is easily possible. The traditional date remains the most natural reading, and nothing in the book's message depends on settling it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ezra came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which was in the seventh year of the king. For on the first day of the first month he began to go up from Babylonia, and on the first day of the fifth month he came to Jerusalem, for the good hand of his God was on him. For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four months, nine hundred miles, with families, animals and a great deal of gold. He began on the first day of the first month — the day, as it happens, on which Moses was told to set up the tabernacle and did (Exod 40:2, 17). Whether Ezra chose the date for that reason we are not told, but a scribe who knew the law as he did could hardly have missed it. (The caravan actually left the river Ahava on the twelfth, after a halt to gather Levites and to fast; 8:31 gives that date.)

The good hand of his God: good, this time, not only powerful but kind. The hand that could have crushed a small party on the desert roads kept it instead.

Verse 10, which this half of the book stands on, begins with for: it gives the reason for verse 9. God was not rewarding Ezra's diligence as though it earned something; his hand was on Ezra long before, and the man who had given his life to God's word is the man God's hand rested on. The text sets the two side by side.

Then the verbs. Set his heart is the phrase that runs through 2 Chronicles, where a man either set his heart to seek God or did not (2 Chr 12:14; 30:19), and the word translated study is the Hebrew word for seeking. What is new here is the object: Ezra set his heart to study the law. He looked for God where God had spoken.

And the order: study it, do it, teach it. It will not run the other way round. A man cannot honestly teach what he has not first obeyed, and he cannot obey what he has not first taken the trouble to understand. Most failures in the ministry of the word are failures to keep that order — teaching without studying, which produces nonsense, or teaching without doing, which produces hypocrites.

This is not only a verse for preachers. Every parent teaches, and every believer is watched by someone. Is what I pass on something I have first sat down with, and then lived in? None of us keeps that order perfectly. The Spirit who opens minds to the Scriptures is the one who works it in us, and the Teacher Ezra foreshadows kept it in our place.
verseByVerse.note: The journey took about four months.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–26 — The Law of Your God, Which Is in Your Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Artaxerxes' letter lets any Israelite who freely offers go with Ezra, sends him to examine Judah by the law in his hand, and funds the altar from royal and freewill gold (vv. 11-20). The treasurers must supply him, the temple staff are freed from tax (vv. 21-24), and Ezra is to appoint judges and teach those who do not know God's laws (vv. 25-26).
verseByVerse.theology: Two hands meet in this chapter. The hand of God is on Ezra (vv. 6, 9, 28), and the law of God is in Ezra's hand (v. 14) — which the king himself, in verse 25, calls the wisdom of your God that is in your hand. The man God holds is the man who holds God's word, and a Persian emperor could see the connection.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 25 writes teaching into imperial law: not only judges who know God's statutes, but teaching for those who do not.

verseByVerse.quote: This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, a man learned in matters of the commandments of the LORD and his statutes for Israel: "Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven. Peace. And now I make a decree that anyone of the people of Israel or their priests or Levites in my kingdom, who freely offers to go to Jerusalem, may go with you. For you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to make inquiries about Judah and Jerusalem according to the Law of your God, which is in your hand, and also to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem, with all the silver and gold that you shall find in the whole province of Babylonia, and with the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly for the house of their God that is in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king's letter, verses 12 to 26, is given in the Aramaic it was written in, and the narrator introduces it with a third description of Ezra in six verses: skilled (v. 6), set on the law (v. 10), learned in it (v. 11). The book will not let us forget what kind of man is being sent.

King of kings was the Persian emperor's standard title. The man who styles himself king of kings is commissioning a scribe to teach the law of the one who actually is.

Nobody is conscripted; any who freely offers may go. As in chapter 1, the door is opened and people are left to walk through it.

Which is in your hand. The hand of the LORD was on Ezra; the law of the LORD was in Ezra's hand. And the king understood the scroll he carried was the standard by which Jerusalem was to be examined, not the king's laws or the customs of the province.

And consider who is sending him: the king and his seven counselors. The book of Esther names that council — the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king's face, and sat first in the kingdom (Esth 1:14) — and it was their advice, in the reign of this king's father, that had Queen Vashti deposed by a decree of the Medes and Persians. A generation later the same body of men is voting gold for the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.note: Artaxerxes’ letter (vv. 12–26) is in Aramaic (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: With this money, then, you shall with all diligence buy bulls, rams, and lambs, with their grain offerings and their drink offerings, and you shall offer them on the altar of the house of your God that is in Jerusalem. Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God. The vessels that have been given you for the service of the house of your God, you shall deliver before the God of Jerusalem. And whatever else is required for the house of your God, which it falls to you to provide, you may provide it out of the king's treasury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first use of the money is the altar. Before salaries, before buildings, before anything else: offerings. The king seems to have understood what the house was for.

And then an extraordinary grant of trust. Whatever seems good to you and your brothers to do with the rest of the silver and gold, you may do, according to the will of your God. No accounting to the treasury, no schedule of approved expenditure. Ezra and his colleagues are to decide, and the standard for deciding is the will of their God. The king was willing to be governed, at one remove, by a law he had never read.

The vessels given for the house are to be delivered before the God of Jerusalem, and anything further that the house requires, Ezra may draw from the royal treasury. It is Darius's decree of chapter 6 renewed and enlarged by his grandson.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, Artaxerxes the king, make a decree to all the treasurers in the province Beyond the River: Whatever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, requires of you, let it be done with all diligence, up to 100 talents of silver, 100 cors of wheat, 100 baths of wine, 100 baths of oil, and salt without prescribing how much. Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full for the house of the God of heaven, lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons. We also notify you that it shall not be lawful to impose tribute, custom, or toll on anyone of the priests, the Levites, the singers, the doorkeepers, the temple servants, or other servants of this house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salt without limit. The law required that every grain offering be seasoned with salt, the salt of the covenant with your God (Lev 2:13), and the king's clerks, whether they knew it or not, wrote no ceiling on it.

Then the king's motive, and it is frank. Whatever is decreed by the God of heaven, let it be done in full for the house of the God of heaven, lest his wrath be against the realm of the king and his sons. Artaxerxes is afraid of Israel's God. He does not worship him, but he does not want to be on the wrong side of him, and he is prepared to pay to stay on the right side. It is not faith. It is, however, more sense than many people have.

And the tax exemption: no tribute, custom or toll on any priest, Levite, singer, doorkeeper, temple servant or other servant of the house. The words are the same three that the accusers of chapter 4 used to frighten this very king — tribute, custom, toll (4:13). They are now written down as the things the servants of the house will never have to pay.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "And you, Ezra, according to the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint magistrates and judges who may judge all the people in the province Beyond the River, all such as know the laws of your God. And those who do not know them, you shall teach. Whoever will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be strictly executed on him, whether for death or for banishment or for confiscation of his goods or for imprisonment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wisdom of your God that is in your hand. In verse 14 the king called it the law of your God; here he calls it the wisdom of your God, and he means the same scroll. A Persian emperor has put it well: the law of God is not an arbitrary list of restrictions but his wisdom, written down, and it can be carried in one man's hand.

Two tasks. Appoint judges from among those who already know God's statutes. And those who do not know them, you shall teach. The Persian crown has written teaching into law. Four hundred years earlier Jehoshaphat sent Levites round Judah having the Book of the Law of the LORD with them (2 Chr 17:9); now an emperor sends a scribe to do the same for a province that stretches from the Euphrates to Egypt.

Verse 26 attaches penalties to disobedience — death, banishment, confiscation, prison — for anyone who will not obey the law of your God and the law of the king. That is Persian civil enforcement, and it belongs to a particular moment when a community's religious law was also its civil law under an imperial governor. It is not a pattern for the church, whose Lord gave it no sword and whose weapons, Paul says, are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–28 — Blessed Be the LORD, the God of Our Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra blesses the LORD for putting this into the king's heart and showing him steadfast love, and takes courage to gather leaders for the journey (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The letter was written by a king, the treasury was the king's, and the first thing Ezra does with it is give the credit away. God put the thing into the king's heart. God showed him steadfast love in front of the court. God's hand gave him courage. There is not a word here about his own qualifications, and chapter 7 has just spent five verses listing them.
verseByVerse.examples: At verse 27 the text changes language and voice at once. The king's letter was in Aramaic; Ezra's blessing is in Hebrew, and in the first person. From here to the end of chapter 9 the book is Ezra's own account, in his own words.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king, to beautify the house of the LORD that is in Jerusalem, and who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers. I took courage, for the hand of the LORD my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first words of Ezra's own account are a blessing.

And the first thing he blesses God for is the king's heart. He has just been handed the most generous commission in the book, drafted by a Persian chancery and sealed by the king of kings, and he does not admire the king for it. Who put such a thing as this into the heart of the king. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the LORD (Prov 21:1), and Ezra knows whose hand turned it.

And who extended to me his steadfast love before the king and his counselors, and before all the king's mighty officers. Steadfast love — chesed, the covenant love the singers sang over the foundation in chapter 3 — shown to one man in a room full of Persian officials. God's faithfulness to his people did not stop at the border of the promised land.

I took courage — the word for a man bracing himself, used of Jehoiada before his coup (2 Chr 23:1). Ezra did not feel brave because the letter was generous. He took courage because of whose hand was on him, and then he did the next practical thing, which was to gather people.

The scribe who set his heart to study the law and do it and teach it was a gift to his generation, and a shadow of someone greater: a Teacher who did not need to study the law, because he had given it; who did it perfectly, in the place of all who have not; and who, on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets ... interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself, and then opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:27, 45). Ezra carried the book in his hand. The book is about him.

7.theology:
Verse 10 is the heart of the second half of Ezra, and it begins with for: the good hand of God rested on the man who had set his heart to seek the law. The order of its verbs is fixed — study, do, teach — and every ministry of the word stands or falls by keeping it.

Two hands meet in the chapter. God's hand is on Ezra (vv. 6, 9, 28); God's law is in Ezra's hand (v. 14), which the king himself calls the wisdom of your God (v. 25). And every open door is credited upward: the king's generosity was God putting it into his heart (v. 27). The man who holds God's word is the man God holds, and he gives the credit away.
7.examples:
The whole story of Esther happens between the last verse of chapter 6 and the first verse of chapter 7.

Ezra was descended from Hilkiah, who found the lost Book of the Law in the temple; his descendant carried it back to Jerusalem.

The hand of God is named six times in chapters 7 and 8, every time explaining something that should not have happened.

He left Babylon on the first day of the first month, the day the tabernacle was first set up.

A Persian king called the law of Moses the wisdom of your God, and wrote into his decree that those who did not know it must be taught.

The king wrote no limit on the salt.

The first words of Ezra's own account are a blessing, and they give the credit for the king's generosity to God.

8.title: The Journey of Faith: Fasting, Prayer, and the Treasure Carried to Jerusalem
8.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the heads of their fathers' houses, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylonia, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king:<sup>2</sup>Of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the sons of David, Hattush.<sup>3</sup>Of the sons of Shecaniah, who was of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, with whom were registered 150 men.<sup>4</sup>Of the sons of Pahath-moab, Eliehoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men.<sup>5</sup>Of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men.<sup>6</sup>Of the sons of Adin, Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men.<sup>7</sup>Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men.<sup>8</sup>Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him 80 men.<sup>9</sup>Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah the son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men.<sup>10</sup>Of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men.<sup>11</sup>Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah, the son of Bebai, and with him 28 men.<sup>12</sup>Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men.<sup>13</sup>Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later, their names being Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men.<sup>14</sup>Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zaccur, and with them 70 men.<sup>15</sup>I gathered them to the river that runs to Ahava, and there we camped three days. As I reviewed the people and the priests, I found there none of the sons of Levi.<sup>16</sup>Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight,<sup>17</sup>and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say to Iddo and his brothers and the temple servants at the place Casiphia, namely, to send us ministers for the house of our God.<sup>18</sup>And by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli the son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah with his sons and kinsmen, 18;<sup>19</sup>also Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, 20;<sup>20</sup>besides 220 of the temple servants, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites. These were all mentioned by name.<sup>21</sup>Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods.<sup>22</sup>For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him."<sup>23</sup>So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty.<sup>24</sup>Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their kinsmen with them.<sup>25</sup>And I weighed out to them the silver and the gold and the vessels, the offering for the house of our God that the king and his counselors and his lords and all Israel there present had offered.<sup>26</sup>I weighed out into their hand 650 talents of silver, and silver vessels worth 200 talents, and 100 talents of gold,<sup>27</sup>20 bowls of gold worth 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold.<sup>28</sup>And I said to them, "You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers.<sup>29</sup>Guard them and keep them until you weigh them before the chief priests and the Levites and the heads of fathers' houses in Israel at Jerusalem, within the chambers of the house of the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So the priests and the Levites took over the weight of the silver and the gold and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.<sup>31</sup>Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way.<sup>32</sup>We came to Jerusalem, and there we remained three days.<sup>33</sup>On the fourth day, within the house of our God, the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites, Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui.<sup>34</sup>The whole was counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded.<sup>35</sup>At that time those who had come from captivity, the returned exiles, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and as a sin offering twelve male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>36</sup>They also delivered the king's commissions to the king's satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, and they aided the people and the house of God.
8.overview: Ezra lists those who travelled with him — priests, a son of David, and twelve lay families, 1,496 men — and at the Ahava canal finds that not one of them is a Levite. He sends a scripted delegation to Casiphia and, by the good hand of our God, thirty-eight Levites and 220 temple servants come (vv. 1-20). He proclaims a fast, ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers, because he had told the king that God's hand is for good on all who seek him and against all who forsake him — and God listened (vv. 21-23). He weighs out a fortune in silver and gold to priests and Levites — you are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy — to be guarded until it is weighed in Jerusalem (vv. 24-30). God delivers the caravan from the enemy and from ambushes; in Jerusalem the whole is weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded; offerings are made for all Israel and the king's orders delivered (vv. 31-36).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — I Found There None of the Sons of Levi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra lists the families who went with him (vv. 1-14). At the Ahava canal he finds no Levites, sends a scripted delegation to Casiphia, and by God's good hand Levites and temple servants come (vv. 15-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The problem of 2:40 has not gone away in eighty years: the first return brought seventy-four Levites, and this one, at first, brought none. The men whose work was the hard daily service of the house would not leave Babylon for it. Ezra did not set off without them and hope. He stopped the caravan for three days and went and asked.
verseByVerse.examples: Sherebiah was a last-minute recruit, fetched from Casiphia because the caravan was short of Levites. Years later, when Ezra stood on a wooden platform in Jerusalem and read the law to the whole people, Sherebiah was one of the Levites who helped the people to understand the Law (Neh 8:7). The man who was found almost by accident became one of the book's teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses, and this is the genealogy of those who went up with me from Babylonia, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king: Of the sons of Phinehas, Gershom. Of the sons of Ithamar, Daniel. Of the sons of David, Hattush. Of the sons of Shecaniah, who was of the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, with whom were registered 150 men. Of the sons of Pahath-moab, Eliehoenai the son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men. Of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men. Of the sons of Adin, Ebed the son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men. Of the sons of Elam, Jeshaiah the son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men. Of the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah the son of Michael, and with him 80 men. Of the sons of Joab, Obadiah the son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men. Of the sons of Bani, Shelomith the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men. Of the sons of Bebai, Zechariah, the son of Bebai, and with him 28 men. Of the sons of Azgad, Johanan the son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men. Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later, their names being Eliphelet, Jeuel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men. Of the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zaccur, and with them 70 men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With me. The list is Ezra's own: the people he travelled with, whose names he knew.

First the priests — Gershom of the line of Phinehas, Daniel of the line of Ithamar — and then a name that matters: Of the sons of David, Hattush. First Chronicles traces Hattush several generations down from Zerubbabel (1 Chr 3:19-22). The house of David has no throne and no kingdom, but it has a member walking in this caravan, and somebody still knew exactly whose descendant he was. The promise that David's house would stand for ever (2 Sam 7:16) was being carried, without a crown, along a desert road toward the Son of David in whom it would be kept (Luke 1:32-33).

Then twelve lay families, each head named and its men counted. (Zattu and Bani in verses 5 and 10 are missing from the Hebrew and supplied from the Septuagint; a word had probably dropped out in copying.) They come to 1,496 men, with wives and children besides, a small company beside the forty-two thousand of chapter 2.

And almost every family name on this list is a family name from that list. The sons of Parosh, of Pahath-moab, of Zattu, of Adin, of Elam: their cousins went home with Zerubbabel eighty years before. These are the branches that stayed behind, and now, two or three generations later, they are following. Some families take two journeys to get home.

The text says so itself at verse 13. Of the sons of Adonikam, those who came later. Six hundred and sixty-six of Adonikam's family went home with Zerubbabel (2:13). The rest of them — Eliphelet, Jeuel, Shemaiah and sixty men — are described exactly as what they were: the ones who came later. God's timetable for a family is not always the same for every member of it.

verseByVerse.quote: I gathered them to the river that runs to Ahava, and there we camped three days. As I reviewed the people and the priests, I found there none of the sons of Levi. Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight, and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say to Iddo and his brothers and the temple servants at the place Casiphia, namely, to send us ministers for the house of our God. And by the good hand of our God on us, they brought us a man of discretion, of the sons of Mahli the son of Levi, son of Israel, namely Sherebiah with his sons and kinsmen, 18; also Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari, with his kinsmen and their sons, 20; besides 220 of the temple servants, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites. These were all mentioned by name.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None. Not a single Levite in the caravan. It is the problem of chapter 2 in a sharper form: the first return had brought seventy-four Levites to more than four thousand priests (2:40), and this one had brought nobody at all. The men whose work was the carrying, the cleaning, the slaughtering, the teaching — the daily, heavy, unglamorous service of the house — had settled in Babylon and were not coming.

Ezra could have gone without them. He stopped instead. Then I sent for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam, leading men, and for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were men of insight — eleven envoys, three of them called Elnathan, which says something about the popular names of that generation — and sent them to Iddo, the leading man at the place Casiphia, telling them what to say.

He scripted the approach. A request for ministers is too important to leave to improvisation.

Remember the name Sherebiah. Years later, when Ezra read the law aloud to the city, Levites went among the crowd and helped the people to understand the Law (Neh 8:7-8), and Sherebiah is on that list. The man fetched at the last minute went on to explain the book.

The temple servants came too, whom David and his officials had set apart to attend the Levites — an order of service that went back five hundred years to David's organising of the house, still recognised and still answering when called.

And Ezra does not credit his own recruiting. By the good hand of our God on us. The people who join a work of God are also his gift.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–23 — I Was Ashamed to Ask the King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Ahava Ezra proclaims a fast to seek a safe journey, ashamed to ask for soldiers after what he had told the king, and God listens (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: What Ezra told the king is 2 Chronicles in one sentence. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you (2 Chr 15:2): seek and forsake, the two great verbs of that book, and Ezra had said them to a Persian emperor. Having said them, he had to travel as though they were true.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra is honest enough to write that he was ashamed — not of trusting God, but of being seen to contradict himself. Nehemiah, years later, accepted an armed escort from the same king (Neh 2:9), and the Bible does not rebuke either man. Ezra had put his words on record before the court, and the fast was what integrity looked like once the words had been said.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river Ahava, that we might humble ourselves before our God, to seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our goods. For I was ashamed to ask the king for a band of soldiers and horsemen to protect us against the enemy on our way, since we had told the king, "The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him, and the power of his wrath is against all who forsake him." So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Humble ourselves, and seek — the shape of the promise God gave at the dedication of the first temple, if my people ... humble themselves, and pray and seek my face (2 Chr 7:14). They had a nine-hundred-mile road ahead, children, and a fortune in gold. They went on their faces by the canal.

He was ashamed: not of God, and not above asking for help. He had told the Persian court that his God protects those who seek him. To ask for cavalry a few weeks later would have told the king what Ezra actually believed.

Seek and forsake are the two great verbs of 2 Chronicles, joined by the prophet Azariah (2 Chr 15:2). Ezra had preached the theology of that whole book to a pagan emperor; now he had to travel as though it were true.

That is a kind of faith most believers know something about: the faith that has said something out loud, in front of people who are watching, and now has to live up to it. The words were easy at court. They were harder at the edge of the desert with the children loaded on the donkeys.

This is not a rule that faith refuses soldiers. Nehemiah, sent by the same king thirteen years later, travelled with officers of the army and horsemen (Neh 2:9), and nobody rebukes him. Ezra's case was particular: he had said a particular thing, and integrity required him to stand on it. So he did what faithful people do with the fear that remains after they have made their decision. He took it to God.

So we fasted and implored our God for this, and he listened to our entreaty. It is the word used when God was moved by the prayer of Manasseh in chains (2 Chr 33:13). The God who let himself be entreated by the worst king in Judah let himself be entreated by a frightened scribe beside a canal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–36 — The Weight of Everything Was Recorded
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra weighs out the treasure to twelve priests and Levites, holy men to guard holy things until it is weighed in Jerusalem (vv. 24-30). God delivers them on the road (v. 31); in Jerusalem everything is weighed and recorded, offerings are made for all Israel, and the king's orders delivered (vv. 32-36).
verseByVerse.theology: Holy people carrying holy things. Ezra told the treasurers that they were holy to the LORD as well as the vessels — both set apart, both belonging to God — and then he gave them a very practical instruction: guard it, and have it weighed at the other end. Holiness and accountability are not rivals. The more sacred the trust, the more carefully it is counted.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 31 does not say there were no enemies. It says God delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way. There were ambushes on the road. The prayer at Ahava was not answered by an empty desert; it was answered by a God whose hand was stronger than the hands that lay in wait.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests: Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their kinsmen with them. And I weighed out to them the silver and the gold and the vessels, the offering for the house of our God that the king and his counselors and his lords and all Israel there present had offered. I weighed out into their hand 650 talents of silver, and silver vessels worth 200 talents, and 100 talents of gold, 20 bowls of gold worth 1,000 darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold. And I said to them, "You are holy to the LORD, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers. Guard them and keep them until you weigh them before the chief priests and the Levites and the heads of fathers' houses in Israel at Jerusalem, within the chambers of the house of the LORD." So the priests and the Levites took over the weight of the silver and the gold and the vessels, to bring them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A careful reader will stop here, because Sherebiah and Hashabiah were introduced six verses ago as Levites, not priests. And verse 30 says it was the priests and the Levites who took charge of the treasure. The likeliest sense is that Ezra appointed twelve leading priests and, alongside them, these two Levites with ten of their kinsmen — priests and Levites sharing the charge. The rest of the passage requires it.

Then he weighed the treasure out to them, and the figures are enormous: six hundred and fifty talents of silver — something over twenty tonnes — silver vessels worth two hundred talents, a hundred talents of gold, twenty gold bowls worth a thousand darics, and two vessels of fine bright bronze as precious as gold. All of it to be carried nine hundred miles without an escort.

You are holy, and the vessels are holy. They were not couriers who happened to carry religious property; they were holy men entrusted with holy things.

And then the most practical sentence imaginable: guard them and keep them until you weigh them. Weighed out at Ahava, weighed in at Jerusalem. The holiness of the trust did not make the accounting unnecessary. It made it essential.

Anyone who handles what belongs to God, money given for his work, the care of his people, the teaching of his word, should hear both halves in that order. First, you are holy to the LORD, set apart by him and not by your own diligence; then, it will be weighed at the other end.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds and a daric about 1/4 ounce (ESV notes): 650 talents of silver is over 24 tons.

verseByVerse.quote: Then we departed from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and from ambushes by the way. We came to Jerusalem, and there we remained three days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four months of road in one honest sentence. There were people waiting for a caravan carrying twenty tonnes of silver, and they waited in vain.

The prayer at Ahava was not answered by an empty desert. It was answered by a stronger hand. Two hands are in the verse: the hand of our God on us, and the hand of the enemy against us, and the first held.

That is usually how God answers the prayer for protection. Not by removing every threat from the road, but by bringing his people through the threats. A believer who expects the first will be disillusioned; a believer who expects the second will find it true.

That hand is now counted six times in two chapters — on Ezra before the king, on him for the road, on him when he took courage, on the caravan when the Levites came, the hand for good on all who seek him, and the hand on the road (7:6, 9, 28; 8:18, 22, 31).

After four months, three days to rest before anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourth day, within the house of our God, the silver and the gold and the vessels were weighed into the hands of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah, and with him was Eleazar the son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites, Jozabad the son of Jeshua and Noadiah the son of Binnui. The whole was counted and weighed, and the weight of everything was recorded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four named men received it, two priests and two Levites — the same balance of offices that carried it.

And the first name is one to linger over. Nehemiah gives his descent: Meremoth the son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz (Neh 3:4). When the first returnees arrived eighty years earlier, the sons of Hakkoz could not find their registration and were barred from the priesthood until a priest could consult Urim and Thummim (2:61-63).

Now a son of Hakkoz is called Meremoth the priest, standing in the house of God with the treasure weighed into his hands. The text does not tell us how the question was settled. It simply shows us the family that could not find its name in the register, eighty years later, entrusted with the gold of the house. The door that was shut until had opened.

The weight of everything, carried nine hundred miles past ambushes, came out right on the scales. Nothing was missing, and the fact was written down.

Paul would write that he took pains with the collection he was carrying to Jerusalem so that no one should blame us about this generous gift (2 Cor 8:20). Ezra had the same instinct five centuries earlier. The honour of God was bound up with the honesty of the men carrying his gold.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time those who had come from captivity, the returned exiles, offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel, twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and as a sin offering twelve male goats. All this was a burnt offering to the LORD. They also delivered the king's commissions to the king's satraps and to the governors of the province Beyond the River, and they aided the people and the house of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve bulls and twelve goats for all Israel, and ninety-six rams — eight for each tribe. Like the returnees of chapter 6, this company offers for every tribe, though it came from only a few. They would not let Israel shrink to the size of whoever had made the journey.

The chapter has two words that belong together. At Ahava, Ezra was ashamed to ask the king for protection, because he had said God would guard those who seek him. And he told the priests to guard the treasure until it was weighed in Jerusalem. Five centuries later, writing from a prison with his own life nearly spent, the apostle put both words in one sentence: But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me (2 Tim 1:12). Ezra's gold came out right on the scales because a hand was on the caravan. Everything a believer has entrusted to Christ will come out right on the last day for the same reason: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

8.theology:
Ezra's words to the king in verse 22 are the two great verbs of 2 Chronicles — seek and forsake (2 Chr 15:2) — said to a pagan emperor, and the fast at Ahava is what integrity looks like once such words have been said in public. The prayer was answered not by an empty road but by deliverance from ambushes by the way (v. 31): God's protection runs through danger, not around it.

Verses 24-34 bind holiness to accountability. The men and the gold are both holy to the LORD, and both are weighed at the other end. The more sacred a trust, the more carefully it is counted — and Paul's words about the deposit Christ guards until that day (2 Tim 1:12) are this chapter's shape carried into the gospel.
8.examples:
There was not one Levite in the caravan, so Ezra stopped for three days and sent to ask.

Three of the eleven men he sent were called Elnathan.

Sherebiah, recruited at the last minute, later helped the whole city understand the law when it was read (Neh 8:7).

Ezra wrote that he was ashamed to ask for soldiers after telling the king his God protected those who seek him.

Nehemiah later took an armed escort from the same king, and the Bible rebukes neither man.

There were ambushes on the road, and the caravan came through them.

Twenty tonnes of silver travelled nine hundred miles and came out right on the scales in the house of God.

9.title: Ezra's Great Prayer: Intercessory Identification and the Gravity of Sin
9.text: <sup>1</sup>After these things had been done, the officials approached me and said, "The people of Israel and the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations, from the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites.<sup>2</sup>For they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands. And in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost."<sup>3</sup>As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled.<sup>4</sup>Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the faithlessness of the returned exiles, gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice.<sup>5</sup>And at the evening sacrifice I rose from my fasting, with my garment and my cloak torn, and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God,<sup>6</sup>saying: "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt has mounted up to the heavens.<sup>7</sup>From the days of our fathers to this day we have been in great guilt. And for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame, as it is today.<sup>8</sup>But now for a brief moment favor has been shown by the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a secure hold within his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes and grant us a little reviving in our slavery.<sup>9</sup>For we are slaves. Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love before the kings of Persia, to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God, to repair its ruins, and to give us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.<sup>10</sup>"And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments,<sup>11</sup>which you commanded by your servants the prophets, saying, 'The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands, with their abominations that have filled it from end to end with their uncleanness.<sup>12</sup>Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons, and never seek their peace or prosperity, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.'<sup>13</sup>And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, seeing that you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved and have given us such a remnant as this,<sup>14</sup>shall we break your commandments again and intermarry with the peoples who practice these abominations? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape?<sup>15</sup>O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this."
9.overview: Officials report that people, priests and Levites, with the leaders foremost, have married into the households of the peoples of the land named in the law's list (vv. 1-2). The issue is worship, not blood: the law forbade such marriages because they would turn away your sons from following me (Deut 7:4), and Ruth the Moabite is David's great-grandmother. Ezra tears his clothes, pulls out his own hair, and sits appalled till the evening sacrifice, joined by those who tremble at God's words (vv. 3-4). Then he kneels and prays, confessing our iniquities, thanking God for a brief reviving, and ending with no request at all (vv. 5-15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The officials report the mixed marriages, with the leaders foremost (vv. 1-2). Ezra tears his garments and sits appalled, and those who tremble at God's words gather round him until the evening sacrifice, when he kneels to pray (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The list in verse 1 is the law's list. Deuteronomy names the nations of Canaan (Deut 7:1) and, separately, Ammon, Moab and Egypt (23:3-7); several of those peoples had long since ceased to exist. The officials are describing their neighbours in the vocabulary of the Torah, and the Torah had given the reason: they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4). The issue was never blood. Ruth was a Moabite, and she is David's great-grandmother — because she said your God my God (Ruth 1:16).
verseByVerse.examples: Nehemiah, facing the same sin, pulled out other men's hair (Neh 13:25); Ezra pulled out his own.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things had been done, the officials approached me and said, "The people of Israel and the priests and the Levites have not separated themselves from the peoples of the lands with their abominations, from the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, the Ammonites, the Moabites, the Egyptians, and the Amorites. For they have taken some of their daughters to be wives for themselves and for their sons, so that the holy race has mixed itself with the peoples of the lands. And in this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ezra has been in Jerusalem some months, the treasure weighed and the king's letters delivered, when officials come with the worst news he could hear.

Several peoples on their list had not existed as nations for centuries. This is the law's list, the nations of Deuteronomy 7 with the Ammonites, Moabites and Egyptians of Deuteronomy 23. The officials describe their neighbours in the vocabulary of the Torah; somebody had been reading the book Ezra brought.

The ESV's footnote gives the Hebrew as "offspring": the holy offspring, close to Isaiah's phrase for the stump left standing when the tree of Israel was cut down: The holy seed is its stump (Isa 6:13). The remnant that had survived the exile was the seed God had kept alive for the future, and now it was being scattered into the fields around it.

It is essential to be clear about what the problem was, or this chapter and the next will be badly misread. It was never race. The law that forbade these marriages gave its reason in the same breath: for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4). The concern was a household's worship, not its ancestry. Moabites are on the officials' list — and Ruth was a Moabite, and she is the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:17), because she said to Naomi your people shall be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16). And three chapters ago the Passover was eaten by every one who had joined them and separated himself from the uncleanness of the peoples of the land (6:21). The door was open to anyone who came to the LORD. What the officials reported was the reverse: Israelites marrying into households that kept their gods.

And the worst line comes last. In this faithlessness the hand of the officials and chief men has been foremost. The leaders had led. The men who should have guarded the community were the ones who had broken the fence first.

What does this mean for a Christian deciding whom to marry? Not that marriage across a line of race or nation is wrong: Moses himself married a Cushite woman, and God rebuked those who spoke against him for it (Num 12:1-9). What carries over is the reason Deuteronomy gave, worship. A believer belongs to the Lord who bought him, and is free to marry only in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39), because marriage is a shared life before God. For those already married to someone who does not share their faith, the next chapter raises the hard question, and the apostle's answer is plain: stay, and love (1 Cor 7:12-16).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as I heard this, I tore my garment and my cloak and pulled hair from my head and beard and sat appalled. Then all who trembled at the words of the God of Israel, because of the faithlessness of the returned exiles, gathered around me while I sat appalled until the evening sacrifice. And at the evening sacrifice I rose from my fasting, with my garment and my cloak torn, and fell upon my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
No committee, no inquiry, no statement. He tore both layers of his clothes, pulled out his own hair and beard, and sat on the ground unable to move.

Nehemiah dealt with the same sin a generation later, and the contrast is instructive. I confronted them and cursed them and beat some of them and pulled out their hair (Neh 13:25). Nehemiah pulled out other people's hair. Ezra pulled out his own. Both were right to be grieved, and there is a place for Nehemiah's kind of reformer. But Ezra's first instinct was not to punish the guilty. It was to sit down in the dust beside them.

All who trembled at the words of God are the kind Isaiah says God looks at: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isa 66:2). When a leader sits down in grief over sin, they are the ones who come and sit with him. Nobody organised them.

Hours passed. He sat there until the evening sacrifice.

Knees and hands. That is exactly how Solomon prayed at the dedication of the first temple: he knelt on his knees in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven (2 Chr 6:13). Solomon knelt to ask God to hear the prayers of a sinning people toward that house. Ezra kneels in the rebuilt house to make one.

And he waited for the evening sacrifice to do it. His prayer was offered at the hour the lamb was on the altar — the confession of guilt joined to the offering for guilt. By the first century, that afternoon offering had become the hour of prayer, the ninth hour (Acts 3:1). Many Christians have noticed that it was at the ninth hour that another Man, bearing sins that were not his own, cried out My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — None Can Stand Before You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ezra's prayer: shame for the people's guilt from the fathers until now (vv. 6-7); thanks for a brief reviving, since God has not forsaken them (vv. 8-9); confession that they have forsaken his commandments again (vv. 10-14); and the verdict, you are just, with no request (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 9 and 10 are the gospel in two sentences. Our God has not forsaken us — we have forsaken your commandments. The whole of 2 Chronicles ran on the rule that if you forsake him, he will forsake you (2 Chr 15:2), and here is a people who had forsaken him again, confessing that he had not forsaken them.
verseByVerse.examples: The prayer ends without asking for anything: no petition, no proposal, no bargain, only you are just and none can stand before you.

verseByVerse.quote: saying: "O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift my face to you, my God, for our iniquities have risen higher than our heads, and our guilt has mounted up to the heavens. From the days of our fathers to this day we have been in great guilt. And for our iniquities we, our kings, and our priests have been given into the hand of the kings of the lands, to the sword, to captivity, to plundering, and to utter shame, as it is today.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ashamed is the word Ezra used at the river Ahava, when he was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers (8:22). There his shame was before a pagan emperor. Here it is before God, and it is for sins he did not commit.

Watch the pronouns. I am ashamed — and then, in the same breath, our iniquities, our guilt. Ezra had been in the country a few months. He was not among the guilty. He had every right to say their iniquities, and he never once does. From the first sentence to the last, the guilty party in this prayer is we.

That is what intercession looks like. Not a righteous man reporting other people's failings to God, but a man standing so close to the people he serves that he cannot tell their sin from his own before the throne.

And the picture is a flood. Iniquities risen higher than our heads, guilt mounted up to the heavens. Sin here is not a list of separate offences that could be ticked off one by one; it is water rising over a drowning man.

He sets the present sin inside the whole history. The exile was not bad luck; it was this, the same pattern, and the people standing in Jerusalem are its survivors — as it is today. A man who confesses only the latest sin has not understood the sin.

verseByVerse.quote: But now for a brief moment favor has been shown by the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant and to give us a secure hold within his holy place, that our God may brighten our eyes and grant us a little reviving in our slavery. For we are slaves.
