Yet our God has not forsaken us in our slavery, but has extended to us his steadfast love before the kings of Persia, to grant us some reviving to set up the house of our God, to repair its ruins, and to give us protection in Judea and Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then, in the middle of the confession, the prayer turns to grace, because the sin cannot be measured until the mercy is measured.

A brief moment. It had been eighty years since Cyrus's decree, and to Ezra it was a moment — a breath of mercy after centuries of judgment.

A secure hold is, the ESV note says, in Hebrew "nail, or tent-pin": something driven into the ground that will take a rope and hold. The remnant had not been given a palace in God's holy place. It had been given a peg — a foothold, a place to fasten to. That was enough to hang a life on.

That our God may brighten our eyes. The eyes of a starving man, or a man in the dark, brightening. A little reviving. Not a great restoration; a little life coming back into dead limbs. Every phrase is modest, and every phrase is gratitude.

For we are slaves. They were still subjects of Persia, paying its tribute, living in a province of its empire. The return had not ended their bondage.

Our God has not forsaken us. Hold that sentence, because the next verse will say the opposite of the people. And protection is, the ESV note says, in Hebrew "a wall." There was no wall around Jerusalem yet; Nehemiah would not build it for another thirteen years. Ezra thanks God for a wall that did not exist in stone, because God had already put one around them.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O our God, what shall we say after this? For we have forsaken your commandments, which you commanded by your servants the prophets, saying, 'The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands, with their abominations that have filled it from end to end with their uncleanness. Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons, and never seek their peace or prosperity, that you may be strong and eat the good of the land and leave it for an inheritance to your children forever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall we say. He runs out of words. After all the mercy of the last two verses, there is nothing to say except the truth.

And set this beside the verse before it. Our God has not forsaken us (v. 9). We have forsaken your commandments (v. 10). The two sentences stand side by side in the prayer, and between them is the whole story of grace.

A reader who has come through 2 Chronicles knows the rule those two verbs usually follow. The prophet Azariah stated it to Asa: if you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you (2 Chr 15:2). By that rule, a people who forsook God's commandments should have been forsaken. Ezra confesses that they had forsaken him, and that he had not forsaken them. The rule had been broken — from God's side, in mercy.

Then he quotes the commandments they had broken, and what he quotes is not one verse but the law's whole voice gathered up: The land that you are entering, to take possession of it, is a land impure with the impurity of the peoples of the lands — the language of Leviticus, where the land itself is said to have become unclean and vomited out its inhabitants (Lev 18:24-25). Therefore do not give your daughters to their sons, neither take their daughters for your sons — Deuteronomy 7:3. And never seek their peace or prosperity — Deuteronomy 23:6, which was said of the Ammonites and the Moabites, both of whom are on the officials' list.

He attributes all of it to your servants the prophets, and Moses was the first of them. The law and the prophets spoke with one voice about a household's worship, and the people in Jerusalem had heard it and done the opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: And after all that has come upon us for our evil deeds and for our great guilt, seeing that you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved and have given us such a remnant as this, shall we break your commandments again and intermarry with the peoples who practice these abominations? Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape? O LORD, the God of Israel, you are just, for we are left a remnant that has escaped, as it is today. Behold, we are before you in our guilt, for none can stand before you because of this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Less than our iniquities deserved. The exile was terrible — the burned city, the dead, the seventy years — and Ezra says it was less than they deserved. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities (Ps 103:10). And having been let off so lightly, they had gone straight back to the sin that caused it. Again. That is the word that breaks him.

Would you not be angry with us until you consumed us, so that there should be no remnant, nor any to escape? The question is not rhetorical. He is asking whether God would be within his rights to finish them, and he knows the answer.

You are just. It is the confession Rehoboam and his princes made when Shishak was at the gates — The LORD is righteous (2 Chr 12:6) — the first time in 2 Chronicles that anyone humbled himself. A confession that begins by agreeing with God's verdict is the kind God has always heard.

And there the prayer ends. There is no request. He does not ask God to forgive them, or to spare them, or to show them what to do. He lays the guilt down in front of a just God and says that nobody can stand, and stops.

It is the exact place where a psalm pauses: If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? (Ps 130:3). Ezra had reached that sentence, and he did not presume to say the next one. He left it to God.

God has said it. But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Ps 130:4). And the reason he can say it without being unjust is the Man who, at the hour of the evening prayer, stood where Ezra's people could not stand, carried iniquities that had risen higher than all our heads, and was forsaken so that we would not be. Now the verb has changed. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand (Rom 5:2). None could stand. In him, we stand.

9.theology:
Ezra confesses sins he did not commit, in the first person plural, from the first sentence to the last. That is intercession: standing so close to the people that their guilt cannot be told from one's own before God. It is the shadow of the one Intercessor who bore sins that were not his.

Verses 9-10 put the gospel in two sentences — our God has not forsaken us; we have forsaken your commandments. By the rule of 2 Chronicles 15:2 the second should have produced the opposite of the first. Mercy broke the rule from God's side.

And the prayer stops at none can stand before you, exactly where Psalm 130 asks who could stand? God answers with the next verse, and the New Testament finishes the thought: this grace in which we stand (Rom 5:2).
9.examples:
The officials described their neighbours with a list of nations that had not existed for centuries — the list in Deuteronomy.

Ruth was a Moabite, and she is David's great-grandmother, because she said your God my God.

Nehemiah pulled out other people's hair over this sin; Ezra pulled out his own.

Nobody organised the people who trembled at God's word; they came and sat down with him.

Ezra knelt and spread his hands exactly as Solomon had at the dedication of the first temple.

He was not among the guilty, and he never once said their sin.

He thanked God for a wall thirteen years before Nehemiah built one.

The prayer asks for nothing.

10.overview:
While Ezra prays, a great assembly gathers, and Shecaniah, from a family on the coming list, confesses the sin and still hopes, proposing a covenant to put away the foreign wives (vv. 1-4). Under oath and summons the people assemble in the December rain, confess, and ask that the cases be heard town by town; four men dissent (vv. 5-15). Examiners finish in three months, a year to the day after Ezra left Babylon, and the book ends with the list of 111 men and their children (vv. 16-44).

The issue was worship, not blood — Ruth the Moabite is in David's line, and anyone who left the peoples' uncleanness was welcome (6:21). And for a Christian the New Testament answers the chapter directly: a believer married to an unbeliever should not divorce, for the spouse is made holy and the children ... are holy (1 Cor 7:12-14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Even Now There Is Hope for Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Ezra prays and weeps, a very great assembly of men, women and children gathers to him, and Shecaniah confesses the sin, holds out hope, and proposes a covenant to put away the foreign wives (vv. 1-4). Ezra puts the people under oath, fasts through the night, and every exile is summoned to Jerusalem within three days, on pain of forfeiture and exclusion (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 2 puts confession and hope in one breath, and repentance needs both: confession without hope becomes despair, and hope without confession becomes presumption. The hope rests on God, not on the reform about to be made; they turn back because he is still the God who kept a remnant for himself. And the man who said it came from a family on the list.
verseByVerse.examples: Ezra's night without bread or water is Moses' fast after the golden calf: I neither ate bread nor drank water, because of all the sin that you had committed (Deut 9:18). The leader grieves longest for the sin he did not commit, and does it where nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: While Ezra prayed and made confession, weeping and casting himself down before the house of God, a very great assembly of men, women, and children, gathered to him out of Israel, for the people wept bitterly. And Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, of the sons of Elam, addressed Ezra: "We have broken faith with our God and have married foreign women from the peoples of the land, but even now there is hope for Israel in spite of this. Therefore let us make a covenant with our God to put away all these wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the commandment of our God, and let it be done according to the Law. Arise, for it is your task, and we are with you; be strong and do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had called no meeting. He lay on the ground in front of the temple and prayed aloud, and the people came, men, women and children, weeping. A leader's honest grief over sin gives other people permission to feel what they have been suppressing.

Shecaniah was of the family of Elam, and a Jehiel of the sons of Elam appears in the list of offenders at the end of the chapter (v. 26) — very possibly his own father. If so, the man who stood up and named the sin was standing inside it, and he still said we.

We have broken faith is the word for treachery in holy things, the breach that cost Saul his throne (1 Chr 10:13) and the last generation its temple (2 Chr 36:14). Yet even now there is hope for Israel. The first real step toward God always has both in it: this is as bad as it is, and he is still who he is.

This proposal is hard to read, and it must be read carefully and honestly, because a Christian reader may be living inside the very situation it describes. First, what it was about: worship, not race. The law forbade these marriages for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut 7:4), and Ezra's prayer has just described the wives' peoples as the peoples who practice these abominations (9:14). Ruth the Moabite, who said your God my God, became David's great-grandmother; and anyone who left the uncleanness of the peoples of the land to worship the LORD was welcome at the Passover (6:21). The problem was households in which the gods of Canaan were being brought into the remnant God had just rescued from exile for precisely that sin.

Second, it belonged to its moment. A tiny community, a few thousand families holding the promise of the Messiah's line in a province of the Persian empire, was being dissolved back into the religion God had exiled it for. Nehemiah reminded them what it had done to Solomon, beloved of God, whom foreign women led into sin (Neh 13:26).

Third, and plainly, it is not what God asks of a Christian today. The apostle answered this question directly for the church: if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him (1 Cor 7:12-13). And he gives the reason, which turns Ezra's situation inside out: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy (7:14). Under the new covenant the holiness runs from the believer into the home, not the uncleanness from the unbeliever into the believer. A Christian who marries is to marry only in the Lord (7:39); a Christian already married to an unbeliever is to stay, and love, and pray. Paul adds two sentences that complete the picture. If the unbelieving partner insists on leaving, let it be so; the believer is not enslaved (7:15). That is desertion, and the Westminster Confession of Faith (24.6) and this commentary hold that it frees the believer. No one is asked to stay where they are in danger either: persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion, the abused should seek safety at once, and the elders help judge each case. And the reason to stay in a willing marriage is hope: how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? (7:16).

Shecaniah's it is your task, and we are with you shows the reform was proposed by the people, not imposed on them. They asked their leader to lead them in what they had already decided.

Was the sending away of foreign wives cruel, and did God approve it? Some think Ezra overreached, since the law forbade making such marriages (Deut 7:3) but did not command dissolving them, and Malachi says God hates divorce (Mal 2:16; that is the KJV's and NKJV's wording, while the ESV renders the difficult Hebrew as a rebuke of the man who does not love his wife but divorces her). But Malachi condemns men who divorced their covenant wives to marry pagans (Mal 2:11, 14), while these marriages had been made in defiance of the covenant, with women who worshipped other gods. The narrator presents the reform as the repentance of a community that was close to losing its faith, as it had before the exile, and records no rebuke. The likeliest reading is that it was right in that unique moment, when the survival of God’s people and the line of the promise were at stake. It is no pattern for Christians: Paul tells a believer not to divorce an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay (1 Cor 7:12–14).

What happened to the wives and children (v. 44)? The text is silent. Most likely they returned to their own families, perhaps with the written certificate the law provided to protect a sent-away wife (Deut 24:1); silence is no licence to imagine they were abandoned, nor to pretend it did not hurt.

A reader who was once sent away, by a parent who left or a spouse who walked out, may find this chapter hard, and need not pretend otherwise. The Bible records this pain without calling it nothing. And the One this book waits for has said of everyone who comes to him: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37). No child of a broken home and no wife put away is outside that promise.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ezra arose and made the leading priests and Levites and all Israel take an oath that they would do as had been said. So they took the oath. Then Ezra withdrew from before the house of God and went to the chamber of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib, where he spent the night, neither eating bread nor drinking water, for he was mourning over the faithlessness of the exiles. And a proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the returned exiles that they should assemble at Jerusalem, and that if anyone did not come within three days, by order of the officials and the elders all his property should be forfeited, and he himself banned from the congregation of the exiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An oath binds a community to its better judgment before its worse judgment can recover.

The public business was done, and he could have gone home satisfied. He went into a side room and fasted through the night instead, as Moses did after the golden calf. (Some scholars use the name of the room's owner, Jehohanan son of Eliashib, to date Ezra later, but the name was common and the point is uncertain.)

The summons is severe: anyone who stays away forfeits his property and is cut off from the congregation. What was at stake was not etiquette but whether the community would remain the people of God at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Trembling Because of This Matter and Because of the Heavy Rain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the December rain the assembly trembles before the house of God. Ezra charges them to confess to the LORD and do his will, and they agree, but ask that the cases be heard at appointed times, town by town, with local elders and judges, since this is no task for one day or two (vv. 9-14). Four men oppose it (v. 15). Named heads of families examine the cases for three months (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The reform is done by procedure, not by mob. A proposal from the people, an oath, a public assembly, a considered delay, local elders and judges, named examiners, and three months of case after case. Serious sin in a community is not dealt with in an afternoon, and the book shows the patience as well as the resolve.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 records dissent and does not explain it. The Bible does not pretend that the people of God were unanimous about the most painful decision they made.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled at Jerusalem within the three days. It was the ninth month, on the twentieth day of the month. And all the people sat in the open square before the house of God, trembling because of this matter and because of the heavy rain. And Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, "You have broken faith and married foreign women, and so increased the guilt of Israel. Now then make confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers and do his will. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from the foreign wives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The twentieth of Chislev was probably in December, when the winter rains have set in, and the text is honest about why they were shaking: because of this matter and because of the heavy rain. Part of it was conviction and part of it was cold. Even in a solemn hour the people of God are still bodies.

In his prayer he had said we. Now, speaking to the people, he says you. Both are right: before God the leader stands inside the people's sin; before the people he must name it without softening it. And the order is exact: confession to the LORD first, then obedience. That order still holds. We confess to a God who has already provided a sacrifice for this very sin (v. 19); for a Christian that sacrifice is Christ, whose perfect obedience is counted as ours where ours falls short, and the turning itself is the work of his Spirit in us (Ezek 36:26-27).
verseByVerse.note: The ninth month (November–December) is the rainy season.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the assembly answered with a loud voice, "It is so; we must do as you have said. But the people are many, and it is a time of heavy rain; we cannot stand in the open. Nor is this a task for one day or for two, for we have greatly transgressed in this matter. Let our officials stand for the whole assembly. Let all in our cities who have taken foreign wives come at appointed times, and with them the elders and judges of every city, until the fierce wrath of our God over this matter is turned away from us." Only Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah opposed this, and Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wet, cold and convicted, they agree, and in the same breath ask for time and local elders. That is not evasion but wisdom. Every case involved a household, a wife, very often children, property, and a town where everyone knew everyone. Cases like that cannot be settled by acclamation in a rainstorm.

The four who opposed are named but not explained. Perhaps they thought the delay too long; perhaps they thought the whole measure too hard; perhaps something else. The narrator neither condemns nor excuses them. A Shabbethai is among the Levites who, years later, helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it (Neh 8:7). If it is the same man, dissent on one hard question did not remove him from the ministry of the word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the returned exiles did so. Ezra the priest selected men, heads of fathers' houses, according to their fathers' houses, each of them designated by name. On the first day of the tenth month they sat down to examine the matter; and by the first day of the first month they had come to the end of all the men who had married foreign women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Named examiners, sitting case by case, for three months: not panic or rumour, but known people taking the time each case requires.

They finished on the first day of the first month, a year to the day after Ezra left Babylon (7:9): the hardest part of his commission was complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–44 — All These Had Married Foreign Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list: priests of the returned houses, who pledge to put away their wives and bring a ram for their guilt (vv. 18-22), Levites, a singer and gatekeepers (vv. 23-24), and eighty-four laymen, family by family (vv. 25-43). The book ends with the children (v. 44).
verseByVerse.theology: The four priestly families on this list (Jeshua, Immer, Harim, Pashhur) are the four that came home in chapter 2 (2:36-39). Not one priestly house was untouched, and the high priest's own family heads the list. Yet the guilt offering they bring is the one Leviticus prescribes for a breach of faith in holy things (Lev 5:15).
verseByVerse.examples: The book ends with the children. For a Christian's own home the New Testament's word runs the other way: a believer married to an unbeliever should not divorce, for as it is, they are holy (1 Cor 7:12-14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were found some of the sons of the priests who had married foreign women: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah, some of the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brothers. They pledged themselves to put away their wives, and their guilt offering was a ram of the flock for their guilt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list begins at the top. Jeshua the son of Jozadak is the high priest who built the altar in chapter 3, whom Zechariah saw standing before the angel in filthy garments (Zech 3:3). Two generations later, his descendants are the first names on the list of the guilty. No house in Israel was too close to the altar to be exempt.

They "gave their hand", a solemn, public pledge. And the offering is exact: the ram Leviticus prescribes for a breach of faith in the holy things of the LORD (Lev 5:15), the very word Shecaniah and Ezra used (vv. 2, 10). The altar built before the temple in chapter 3 was doing what it was built for. There was a sacrifice even for this.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the sons of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah. Of the sons of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah. Of the sons of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah. Of the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (that is, Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer. Of the singers: Eliashib. Of the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the other priestly houses, seventeen priests in all, and after them six Levites, one singer and three gatekeepers.

Two of those Levite names should be held onto: Kelaiah (that is, Kelita), whose other name the narrator stops to give, and Jozabad. When Ezra later read the law to the whole city, the Levites who helped the people to understand the Law included a Jozabad and a Kelita (Neh 8:7). If they are the same men, two Levites who put away their wives that December became, a dozen years on, teachers of the book that had convicted them. Forgiven men make the most careful teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Israel: of the sons of Parosh: Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Hashabiah, and Benaiah. Of the sons of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah. Of the sons of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza. Of the sons of Bebai were Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai. Of the sons of Bani were Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth. Of the sons of Pahath-moab: Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh. Of the sons of Harim: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, Shimeon, Benjamin, Malluch, and Shemariah. Of the sons of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei. Of the sons of Bani: Maadai, Amram, Uel, Benaiah, Bedeiah, Cheluhi, Vaniah, Meremoth, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Mattenai, Jaasu. Of the sons of Binnui: Shimei, Shelemiah, Nathan, Adaiah, Machnadebai, Shashai, Sharai, Azarel, Shelemiah, Shemariah, Shallum, Amariah, and Joseph. Of the sons of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jaddai, Joel, and Benaiah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the laymen, family by family: seven of the sons of Parosh, six of Elam, six of Zattu, four of Bebai, six of Bani, eight of Pahath-moab, eight of Harim, seven of Hashum, twelve more of Bani, thirteen of Binnui, seven of Nebo. Eighty-four men in eleven family groups.

Almost every one of those family names is on the list of chapter 2, and several are on Ezra's own list in chapter 8. These were the grandsons of the people who wept and shouted over the foundation.

The whole list comes to a hundred and eleven men on the ESV's reading of verses 37-38 (the Hebrew can be counted as a hundred and thirteen). Out of tens of thousands it is a small number, but not a small matter: priests, Levites and the heads of the leading families set the direction for everyone else.

And the Bible keeps every name, not to shame them, since they had confessed and brought their offering, but because God deals with people, not categories, and a list of the forgiven is still a list of his.

verseByVerse.quote: All these had married foreign women, and some of the women had even borne children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there the book ends. No feast, no dedication, no summary. A list, and a line about the children.

It is an uncomfortable ending, and it is meant to be. The narrator does not hide the cost. There were women and children in these homes, and the book does not tell us where they went or how they lived. Even the last clause is uncertain: the Hebrew of verse 44 is difficult, and 1 Esdras, a later Greek retelling, reads that they sent the women away with their children. Reform in that hour was real, and it was painful, and Scripture records the pain without pretending it away.

Which is why a Christian must read the last verse of Ezra with the New Testament open. The apostle's word to a believer married to an unbeliever is the opposite of this chapter's covenant: he should not divorce her — because as it is, they are holy (1 Cor 7:12-14). The children of such a home are not to be sent away. They are set apart by a believing parent's teaching and prayers, though each must still come to Christ by his own faith. Paedobaptist brothers read holy as a mark of covenant membership; this commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, reads it as the influence of a believing home, and gladly owns that faithful Christians differ. What changed between Ezra and Paul was not that God grew less holy. It was that the Holy One himself had come, and holiness now spreads outward from those who belong to him.

And the book that ends with foreign wives sent away is followed, in the fullness of time, by a gospel that brings the foreigners in: you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:13).

Not by lowering the standard of this chapter, which was never lower, but by a Bridegroom who took a bride from among the nations, unclean and far off, and instead of putting her away, gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her (Eph 5:25-26). Ezra's community could keep itself holy only by sending the foreigner away. Christ makes the foreigner holy and keeps her.

10.theology:
Shecaniah's even now there is hope (v. 2) holds together what repentance needs: an honest name for the sin and a settled confidence in God's mercy. The guilt offering of v. 19 shows that the hope was not presumption.

The chapter belongs to a unique moment, when a tiny remnant carrying the promise of the Messiah's line was being drawn back into the idolatry it had been exiled for; Malachi condemns the same sin in the same generation (Mal 2:11). The new covenant reverses the direction of the danger: holiness now flows from the believer into the marriage (1 Cor 7:14). The book that ends with foreigners sent away gives way to a gospel in which Christ brings them near (Eph 2:13) and makes his bride holy rather than putting her away (Eph 5:25-27).
10.examples:
The man who first named the sin came from a family on the list, and he still said we, and even now there is hope.
